Some texts "will deploy stereotypical representations of some of these demographic social groups" while others "will consciously seek to challenge stereotypes." You run each technical element through these axes: camera ("Who is shot from a high/low angle? Who gets the close-ups?"), sound ("How does vocal performance construct representation of class / age / gender / ethnicity?"), and mise-en-scène ("Who occupies the foreground? Who is marginalised spatially?").

Mise-en-scène work also includes genre: compare two drama extracts and ask "How does mise-en-scène reinforce genre conventions?", and re-design a scene across social realism, noir crime, teen melodrama and sci-fi dystopia.

concepts/technical-elements.md.body:
# Technical Elements

The four-part toolkit for reading moving image. You drill it all year, and it is tested directly in **Component 2 Section A**. It is also the vocabulary you use in production.

The syllabus frames it as a means, not an end (Syllabus 2027 p.16):

> "Candidates should study a range of texts so that they can discuss, in response to the question, how the following technical elements create specific representations of individuals/groups/events/places, and help to articulate specific messages and values that have social significance."

**Naming alone earns little.** The mark is in technique → meaning → representation. This is the single most repeated correction in the course.

Every exercise routes technique through representation of **class, age, gender, ethnicity**. For the theorists connected to this, see [[concepts/representation]].

## The four elements, per the syllabus (p.16)

### Camera: shots, angle, movement, composition

- **shots** — establishing, master, close-up, mid-shot, long, wide, two-shot, aerial, point-of-view, over-the-shoulder, "and variations of these"
- **angle** — high, low, canted
- **movement** — pan, tilt, track, dolly, crane, steadicam, hand-held, zoom, reverse zoom
- **composition** — framing, rule of thirds, depth of field (deep and shallow focus), focus pulls

Learn these as meaning pairs, not as a list: low angle grants power, canted angle signals dissonance, shallow focus isolates, hand-held destabilizes.

### Sound

- diegetic and non-diegetic, synchronous/asynchronous, sound effects, sound motif, sound bridge, dialogue, voiceover, mode of address / direct address, sound mixing, sound perspective
- **soundtrack** — score, incidental music, themes and stings, ambient sound

Sound is often neglected, so build a vocabulary of sound terminology, e.g. harmony, dissonance, discordance, sound bed, rhythm, crescendo, pitch, timbre. Because it is neglected across the candidature, sound is the cheapest way for a script to stand out.

### Mise-en-scène

- **production design** — location, studio, set design, costume and make-up, properties
- lighting, colour design

> [!important] What is *not* here
> **Acting and performance are not listed under mise-en-scène**, and the syllabus states separately that "acting is not a skill that is assessed in media studies" (p.30). Body language and expression are also absent from the syllabus bullet.

For ESL learners this is the highest-yield element: costume, lighting and colour are visible, nameable, and rich in connotation.

### Editing

"This includes transition of image and sound – continuity and non-continuity systems."

- **cutting** — shot/reverse shot, eyeline match, graphic match, action match, jump cut, crosscutting, parallel editing, cutaway, insert
- **other transitions** — dissolve, fade-in, fade-out, wipe, superimposition, long take, short take, slow motion, ellipsis and expansion of time, post-production, visual effects

> [!important] Commonly misfiled
> **Long take, short take and slow motion are filed under Editing**, not camera.

Editing is invisible until you make it visible — which is what the cut-counting exercise in [[concepts/the-viewing-protocol]] is for.

## How it is examined

Component 2 Section A: an unseen extract "from a TV drama and will last for a maximum of five minutes. It will be played four times. The screening time will last a total of 30 minutes, including note-taking" (Syllabus 2027 p.23). Then 45 minutes of writing, 25 marks.

The syllabus's coverage caveat (p.23):

> "It is acknowledged that not every one of the technical areas will feature in equal measure in any given extract and other areas may also be credited where appropriate… We do not expect each aspect to be covered in the same degree of detail, but as appropriate to the genre and extract provided and to the discussion of the extract's representation."

So a script does not need to hit all four elements evenly. It needs to hit what the extract actually does, and tie each observation to representation.

## The analytical paragraph frame

Expected output shape: technique named → terminology → meaning created → link to representation → link to the question.

This frame is the direct rehearsal for A1 and A4 in [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-assessments|the S1 register]], and it is what CS4, CS6 and CS8 practise.

## Spec note

The 2027 spec screens the extract from **DVD, four times**. Under the 2028–30 syllabus the exam is digital and the extract is embedded in the platform — see [[classes/media-studies/media-studies]] for the straddle. The technical vocabulary transfers unchanged; the **format practice does not**.

entities/bell-hooks.md.body:
# bell hooks

bell hooks (lowercase, as she styled it) is one of the representation theorists in this course.

## Representation theory

Cambridge lists her among the theorists you can use to study the concept of Representation, alongside **Hall, Van Zoonen, Gilroy, and Alvarado**. In media studies, hooks is most often used for the **oppositional gaze**.

## In this course

You study hooks in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-09-the-gaze|L09]], Day 4 (Friday single). The lesson covers the oppositional gaze as refusal and rereading — "who the text never expected to be looking" — closing the gaze topic and leading into CS6.

There is a homework reading extract from hooks (300–400 words, in accessible English with Chinese support).

entities/bill-nichols.md.body:
# Bill Nichols

Bill Nichols is the theorist behind the idea of **documentary modes**. His work is referenced in the Component 3 documentary brief as a way to introduce the six modes of documentary.

## When it becomes relevant

Nichols' modes matter only if you take the **documentary package** for [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-course-map|Component 3]]. The set brief you work on may be restricted to one option or left as a free choice — this will be confirmed in class.

If you do take the documentary brief, the modes are essential: the pitch-feedback stage asks "What mode would be most appropriate," so you need to know the modes before you can pitch.

## How the modes fit

The modes framework answers the core documentary research questions:

- What different kinds of documentaries are there?
- What is the purpose of a documentary?
- What is the audience for documentary?

One way into the same material is to categorise films from a published documentary list: What different categories are listed here? What stories get told? Whose stories get told?

entities/fredric-jameson.md.body:
# Fredric Jameson

Jameson is the only theorist in Component 4 given a full analytical framework rather than just a name.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

"Similarly, and more recently, **Fredric Jameson** diagnoses the postmodern condition as characterised by:" (SoW pp.23–24)

| Symptom | Cambridge's wording |
|---|---|
| **Ahistorical mode** | "lacking a sense of the past – history becomes another set of signifiers which can be played with" |
| **Collapse of high/low** | "A lack of distinction between 'high' and 'low' culture" |
| **Surfaces** | "increasingly there is no time for depth – politics becomes soundbites, protests become slogans, the world is a collection of images" |
| **Affectlessness** | "the predominant mode of irony and 'knowingness' leaves little room for real emotion, but short, sharp intense emotional responses are elicited through surface representations of things of which people have no first-hand experience, e.g.: Brexit, the death of Diana, refugees" |
| **Technologies of reproduction and recirculation** | "e.g.: all social media" |

## How to use this list

Each symptom converts into an essay paragraph: name the symptom, supply a contemporary text, show the symptom operating, and evaluate whether the diagnosis holds.

The list is also exhaustive enough to argue against. The syllabus requires "the arguments for and against understanding some forms of media as postmodern" (Syllabus 2027 p.18), and a five-point checklist gives you a way to show where a text fails to fit.

## Relation to Debord

Cambridge sequences these deliberately: [[entities/guy-debord]] first (1967, spectacle), then "similarly, and more recently, Fredric Jameson." The implied argument is continuity — a diagnosis of image-saturated culture restated for a later moment. Cambridge does not develop the comparison, but you could.

concepts/the-viewing-protocol.md.body:
# The Viewing Protocol

The course's core analytical method, worth building into a routine from week one: **break an extract into its component parts by isolating one element at a time, then reassemble it.**

> "The principle here is to break down an extract from a TV drama into its component parts and then reassemble them in order to reach some insights into how it produces particular meanings."

You will also work through per-element exercises — shot-type drills, freeze-frame deconstruction, sound audits, mise-en-scène audits, editing timelines (see [[concepts/technical-elements]]). Extracts are chosen from within about five years of when you study them, from different organisations and across a mix of genres (see [[concepts/case-study-method]]).

## The four passes

| Pass | What runs | What you focus on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Full extract, ~5 min | Nothing — no response is required yet |
| 2 | Sound down | Mise-en-scène |
| 3 | Sound still off | Camera: shots, angles, movement, composition |
| 4 | Screen covered or blanked | Sound |

The sound pass has its own prompts: What do we hear? Is it diegetic or non-diegetic? What mood is created? How could the music be described? To whom are the voices addressed?

## The editing pass

Editing gets its own move, because it is the element you cannot see:

> "A focus on editing brings many of these elements together – initially it might be useful for learners to count out loud, or tap whenever there is a visual transition, which is a simple exercise, but it makes something potentially 'invisible' become visible."

Follow-up questions: Is it a cut or a mix/dissolve? What's the effect of this? What visual elements are brought together? Does it create continuity? Contrast? Does it reveal something about character? Does it develop the story?

## The reassembly

The protocol is not finished until the parts go back together:

> - What is the function of this opening?
> - How does it set up the beginning of a story?
> - How does it establish character, mood and setting?
> - What kinds of competence does it require of the audience?
> - How are particular representations of individuals, groups, events and places constructed through the technical elements identified?

The last question is the one that converts description into exam marks. It is where the protocol hands off to [[concepts/representation]].

## Choosing the extract

- Openings of first episodes usually work well, because they establish setting, tone, character, and set up some narrative expectations.
- A range of examples is used, including ones that have previously featured in examinations. Building expertise in what to look for and how to articulate it is an iterative process.

Using past exam extracts makes the practice authentic and calibrates you to the real difficulty level.

## Output

You practise the analytical process, possibly in groups and then presenting your findings, and/or individually in a short-form essay. This is formative **(F)** — frequent and low stakes.

## Why it is worth the routine

1. It is direct rehearsal for **Component 2 Section A**, where the extract is screened four times. Four screenings is the exam's own version of this protocol, and if you have practised element-isolation you know what to do with each pass.
2. It **rescues sound**, the element most easily neglected. A dedicated screen-covered pass is the most reliable way to make yourself hear.
3. It **continues from C1**: the approaches and terminology are the same, so the protocol serves both portfolio research and exam analysis.

entities/liesbet-van-zoonen.md.body:
# Liesbet van Zoonen

Liesbet van Zoonen is a media theorist associated with feminist media theory and the representation of gender.

## Representation theory

The concept of Representation is best studied with reference to theories of representation, for which student-friendly materials are available. The theorists you may work with include:

> **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**

This covers the representation of class, age, gender, ethnicity; van Zoonen is the standard reference for the gender strand.

## Where you meet her

You study van Zoonen in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-09-the-gaze|L09]], parts 1–2: gender as performance, worked on two advertisements, before Mulvey's three looks are stated precisely.

entities/guy-debord.md.body:
# Guy Debord

Debord is the anchor for **The Society of the Spectacle** in the [[concepts/postmodern-media]] debate.

## The key claim

> "Guy Debord's 1967 work The Society of the Spectacle is a critique of media-saturated capitalist culture is still relevant in diagnosing aspects of the postmodern condition"

In short: Debord wrote a 1967 critique of media-saturated capitalist culture, still useful for diagnosing aspects of the postmodern condition.

## How to use him

A worked exercise:

> **Exercise:** Watch a TV news story. What features does it have of 'The Society of the Spectacle'?

This turns an abstract diagnosis into observable features of a real text — the kind of anchoring in specific texts or phenomena that marks a sophisticated answer.

## A connection worth making

**Détournement** appears in [[concepts/power-and-the-media]] as a strategy of resistance, without attribution. It comes from the same tradition as Debord: the spectacle is the diagnosis, and détournement is the counter-move. Linking the two gives you a genuine synthesis to draw on.

entities/manuel-alvarado.md.body:
# Manuel Alvarado

Manuel Alvarado is a representation theorist. In A Level media studies he is the standard reference for racial-stereotype categories, usually studied alongside Hall and Gilroy. He is one of the theorists (with Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks and Gilroy) used to teach the concept of representation of class, age, gender and ethnicity.

He is not currently taught at BNDS. Like [[entities/paul-gilroy]], he may be used later to deepen the ethnicity strand of [[concepts/representation]] in the G12 year. Anything decided about this will be confirmed in class.

entities/paul-gilroy.md.body:
# Paul Gilroy

Paul Gilroy is a representation theorist named in the Cambridge-suggested roster for representation theory.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "candidates need to learn the concept of Representation - best done with reference to theories of representation where there is a variety of student-friendly materials available - such as **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**."

This concerns the representation of class, age, gender and ethnicity in Section A analysis.

## Status in the course

Gilroy is not currently taught at BNDS. The S1 representation block ([[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-4-representation|U4]]) uses Hall, van Zoonen, Mulvey and hooks.

entities/roland-barthes.md.body:
# Roland Barthes

> [!note] Taught in two courses
> He appears in two courses for two different arguments. Everything below is Media Studies (9607), where he anchors semiotics and narrative codes. For the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]], where he is a one-sentence statement of [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]], skip to [the last section](#in-the-oxbridge-discussion-group).

The most-used theorist in 9607, and one of two theorists named for the AS year (the other is [[entities/stuart-hall]]). He is the only theorist named in Component 1.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

Two distinct contributions:

**Semiotics — signs, codes and meaning.** The theory hook for C1 research on both briefs: "Relevant theory: semiotics – **Roland Barthes'** ideas about signs, codes and meaning."

**Narrative codes and signification.** In the Component 2 textual-analysis material:

> "This work does not need to be densely theoretical, but there is an opportunity to use some of **Roland Barthes'** narrative codes to provide some explanatory depth… as well as notions of signification – what is **denoted** at a descriptive level, and what is suggested, implied or coded at a **connotative** level"

Barthes here is optional explanatory depth, not required content.

## Where he fits in the course

- **[[concepts/media-language]]** — denotation and connotation is the ladder the whole of Unit 2 climbs. The denotation-before-connotation discipline is built into CS1 in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-01-the-four-key-concepts|L01]] and marked in A1.
- **[[concepts/narrative]]** — the enigma code gives narrative analysis explanatory depth without heavy theory, and connects to the C1 film-opening research question "how does the film establish an enigma from the outset?"
- **C1 research** — signs and codes are the vocabulary for annotating real openings and covers.

## BNDS usage

Taught across [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-02-semiotics-how-images-mean|L02]] and [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-03-sign-types-and-codes|L03]] as the semiotics spine of Unit 2.

## In the Oxbridge Discussion Group

A completely different Barthes here, and a much smaller one: a single sentence, delivered once.

### The claim in one line

Ideology works best when it presents itself as **nature** rather than as a position, so the most ideological text is the one that appears to have no author.

### The quote

> The author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all.

### How that course uses him

Barthes arrives at the end of [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], to name what you have already built out of maps and video-game boundaries — never at the start. He is the cleanest single-sentence statement of [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]]. The ordering matters: the line is compressed enough to be memorized without being understood if it arrives before the examples.

### The connection between the two courses

Both are the same underlying claim about signification in different registers. 9607 teaches denotation and connotation as a method for reading a text; Oxbridge takes the political consequence — that a text which hides its own authorship is doing the most ideological work — and never touches the semiotic apparatus at all. In the two rooms he can look like two different figures.

The Oxbridge quotation is given without a source text, as with every quotation in that course.

entities/marshall-mcluhan.md.body:
# Marshall McLuhan

Named, with [[entities/neil-postman]], as an origin of [[concepts/media-ecology]].

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "The notion of media ecology can be traced back to **Neil Postman** and **Marshall McLuhan**, but its contemporary relevance is clearly driven by the saturation of all aspects of contemporary existence with media and media technologies." (SoW p.25)

That is the complete attribution. The Cambridge documents credit no specific idea, book, or coinage to him — no "the medium is the message," no global village, no hot and cool media.

## Media ecology in the course

Media ecology is a compulsory 30-mark synoptic paper — half of Component 4. The syllabus defines it as "the complex environments within which media texts, producers, distributors, technologies and audiences exist" (Syllabus 2027 p.19).

entities/neil-postman.md.body:
# Neil Postman

Named, with [[entities/marshall-mcluhan]], as the origin of [[concepts/media-ecology]].

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "The notion of media ecology can be traced back to **Neil Postman** and **Marshall McLuhan**, but its contemporary relevance is clearly driven by the saturation of all aspects of contemporary existence with media and media technologies." (SoW p.25)

This is the complete attribution. No specific idea, work, or argument is credited to him — no *Amusing Ourselves to Death*, no technopoly, no distinction between the typographic and televisual mind.

## The method for media ecology

For media ecology, Cambridge gives a **method** rather than a theory (SoW pp.25–26):

- historical contrast — "What did the media landscape look like before 1990?" against your own media diary
- a premise — contemporary life is saturated with media and "mediatised"
- a temporal orientation — "contrasting the present with the past, and analysing the present in order to develop ideas about the future"

The before/after contrast does most of the analytical work, and the exam rewards "informed, imaginative analysis" (SoW p.26) grounded in contemporary evidence. Separately, the syllabus requires you to "use key theories of media studies" (Syllabus 2027 p.13).

The current form of this topic uses a three-era periodization and four structured focus areas — see [[concepts/media-ecology]].

Grade 12, Semester 4 content. See [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-course-map|the course map]].

entities/stuart-hall.md.body:
# Stuart Hall

Stuart Hall's ideas come up in this course in two ways: **encoding and decoding**, and **representation**.

## Encoding and decoding

This is an extension activity: exploring Stuart Hall's ideas of encoding and decoding when making sense of a media text. Extension activities are differentiated content for stronger learners, not core AS content.

The standard three reading positions — **dominant, negotiated, oppositional** — are widely taught. Treat them as course-standard knowledge.

Hall's model is a way of thinking about how audiences interpret the media, including how they may interpret the same text in different ways, using a variety of theories or ideologies.

## Representation

Hall is also studied as a **representation theorist**. When you learn the concept of Representation, you can do this with reference to theories of representation, including **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**.

## Where it leads

Encoding/decoding is the bridge from thinking about audiences as a target to thinking about audiences as interpreters. It feeds forward into [[concepts/power-and-the-media]], where the question of whose reading counts becomes the topic itself.

entities/slavoj-zizek.md.body:
# Slavoj Žižek

The only theorist Cambridge names in the [[concepts/power-and-the-media]] debate.

You are asked to consider his idea of the media's "Standard Operating Procedure," and also to test whether that diagnosis still holds: "In the years since the publication of this article, it is now also worth considering how much has changed in terms of increased representation of different ethnicities in media productions - and also analyse how and why degrees of change have occurred." Test the diagnosis rather than citing it as settled.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "Media ownership will be one factor to consider, and there are examples of media outlets being directly influenced, or self-censoring, because of their owners, but more significant will be what **Slavoj Žižek** calls the media's **'Standard Operating Procedure'** – its reproduction of ideological 'truths' about which voices count for more than others, its reduction of complex conflicts to spectacle, and the general reinforcing of 'common sense'." (SoW p.25)

Three mechanisms, all usable as analytical categories:

1. reproduction of ideological "truths" about whose voice counts
2. reduction of complex conflicts to spectacle
3. general reinforcement of "common sense"

## Why Cambridge reaches for him here

The sentence structure is the argument: ownership and self-censorship are the obvious answers to "where does media power live," and Cambridge explicitly says something else is "more significant." The point is that power operates **without anyone issuing an instruction** — through the ordinary, unremarkable procedures by which stories get told.

In an essay, this is the move from a conspiratorial reading (owners dictate content) to a structural one (procedures reproduce common sense). The second is far more defensible and much harder to argue against.

## Connection to spectacle

"Reduction of complex conflicts to spectacle" links directly to [[entities/guy-debord]] in the [[concepts/postmodern-media]] topic — the same concept, used in two of the three debates. Cambridge does not flag the overlap: learn spectacle once and you can use it in both.

shared/bnds-ai-policy.md.body:
# BNDS AI Policy

This is a school-wide policy, from the **A-Level Student Guide 2025-26 §VI** (pp.22–24), within the Academic Honesty Policy. It applies to every course.

Rather than a blanket permit-or-ban, it defines **six graded levels**. Each assignment declares which level applies.

## The six levels (Guide pp.23–24)

| Level | Name | What is allowed |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Human-Only Work | You produce everything without AI help. No disclosure required |
| **1** | AI for Ideation | AI only to clarify the task, surface key terms, or map existing knowledge — **not to generate fresh concepts**. You still do your own brainstorming. Typical: definitions, locating foundational references, checking feasibility, keyword lists for literature searches |
| **2** | AI for Structuring | Level 1 + AI organizes material — outlines, templates, flowcharts. **No full paragraphs, code blocks, calculations or images generated** |
| **3** | AI for Refinement | Levels 1–2 + AI edits or polishes your draft: grammar, style, citation format, code linting. **Keep a before-and-after or tracked-changes file** showing what you accepted |
| **4** | AI Co-Creation | Levels 1–3 + you and AI share the labor. Substantial parts AI-generated or transformed, then shaped by you. **Track who did what and cite the model and version** |
| **5** | AI-Generated for Review | Levels 1–4 + the whole piece is AI-produced, submitted only so humans can critique or annotate it. **Label it "AI-generated"**; grading focuses on your analysis, not the AI text |

> [!important] Always check the AI Level for each assignment
> Some assignments **ban AI entirely** — the handbook names exams and personal reflections — and others actively encourage it.

## Attribution requirements (Guide p.22)

Whenever you use AI, you must:

1. **Cite the tool** — e.g. "Generated with assistance from [AI Tool Name]"
2. **Explain how it was used** — e.g. "Used for brainstorming but all analysis is my own"
3. **Cite the prompt** you used

Your instructor may additionally require a disclaimer or a reflection on AI use.

## Permitted and prohibited (Guide p.22)

**Permitted:** assisting learning (brainstorming, clarifying concepts, summarizing readings, generating practice questions); enhancing productivity (grammar checks, citation formatting, organizing research); encouraging creativity (AI output as a *starting point* for original work, with attribution); developing digital literacy.

**Prohibited:** submitting AI-generated work as your own without citation or permission; using AI to replace independent analysis, original thought or personal reflection unless explicitly allowed; spreading unverified AI content — you must verify AI-generated content for accuracy.

Misuse follows the Academic Honesty Policy: resubmission, grade penalties, or disciplinary action (Guide p.23).

## The Art & Design worked example (Guide p.24)

- **Level 1** — AI summarizes Bauhaus colour theory so you can plan palette experiments
- **Level 2** — AI offers a clean portfolio layout grid (page order, caption placeholders, margins) that you fill with original work
- **Level 3** — AI polishes the grammar of an artist statement and reorganizes paragraphs for flow
- **Level 4** — Midjourney, Stable Diffusion or similar generates an image that you then collage, annotate and contextualize, **detailing the AI's role in the process**

## ⚠ Where school policy meets exam-board policy

These are separate regimes, and the exam board is the stricter authority on assessed work. Both must be satisfied.

| | Position |
|---|---|
| **BNDS** | Six levels; Level 4 co-creation explicitly permitted, including generated images in Art & Design, with attribution |
| **Cambridge 9479 (2028-30)** | AI-generated images permitted **only** with your own role demonstrated and justified — see [[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design]] |
| **Cambridge 9607 (2027)** | *"Cambridge International has a policy on the use of generative AI by candidates in coursework. The inappropriate use of AI should be treated as a form of plagiarism"* (Syllabus 2027 p.30). The 2027 spec does not otherwise address AI; the 2028-30 spec permits it with documented prompts and justification |

**The practical rule for coursework:** BNDS Level 4 may be permissible for classroom tasks, but anything going to Cambridge as assessed coursework is governed by the syllabus for the exam year. Where they differ, the syllabus wins — and the handbook's attribution requirements (cite the tool, explain the use, cite the prompt) are exactly what the 2028-30 Art & Design spec asks for, so satisfying BNDS properly also satisfies Cambridge.

This is the **2025-26** edition of the handbook.

shared/bnds-assessment-framework.md.body:
# BNDS Assessment Framework

The school-wide grading scheme from the **BNDS A-Level Student Guide 2025-26**, applied by every course. This page is the single reference for the rules below. The framework, curving, notice, retake and AI rules are current; syllabus specifics change per subject and per exam year.

## Grade composition

| Category | Weight | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| **Attainment** | **50%** | Major, summative. Syllabus content only, exam conditions, curved to CIE past-paper data; should produce a reliable Forecast Grade. Project completions and portfolio milestones count. |
| **Course Skills** | **20%** | Minor, formative. Skills/content relevant to the syllabus, flexible format: quizzes, drafts, practice tasks, homework. |
| **Learning Behaviour** | **10%** | Glossary upkeep, blog punctuality, screening/feedback participation, case-study contributions, correcting work, submitting on time. |
| **End of Term Exam** | **20%** | Summative, previously covered content, sat in the school exam window (S1 2026-27: Mon 2027-01-11 – Mon 2027-01-18). |

## Notice for assessments

**Attainments carry at least one week's notice** (AL Student Guide p.13). Non-attainment assessments carry **72 hours**.

## Standing rules

- **4–6 attainments per semester**; none in the first two teaching weeks.
- **Attainment dropping** — one per semester, late in the semester, but only if the class has **≥6 attainment grades in MB**, and you have missed none, have no plagiarism or cheating record, no unexcused absences, are always on time, and attend all required grade/programme meetings (Guide p.12). ⚠ **All four courses run four attainments, so no student is eligible to drop one.** This is a result of how the courses are designed, not of your conduct.
- **One grade per week** posted on MB — at least one grade per subject each week (Guide p.12). Learning Behaviour postings fill the weeks with no CS task or attainment.
- **Marking returned within 5 working days** (Guide p.12).
- **Homework capped at 30 minutes per subject per day** (Guide p.13); break homework ≈ 3–4 hours per ten-day holiday.
- **Extensions** must be requested **at least 24 hours before the deadline** (Guide p.13).
- **Absence from an assessment** requires contacting the subject teacher **24 hours before the due time**; illness needs a doctor's note. ⚠ *"If no communication is made with the subject teacher in advance you may be given 0, even if this is due to illness"* (Guide p.8).
- **Late-work cutoff:** three weeks before the last school day of the semester (Guide p.13). For S1 this falls inside the winter break, so the operative date will be confirmed — see [[calendar|school academic calendar]].
- **Assessment content:** only what has been taught and practised — *"You should have seen similar content or formats beforehand"* — though "the context in which the knowledge or skills are applied may be novel" (Guide p.9).
- Formative (CS) tasks placed next to an attainment are **direct practice for it**.
- **Seniors get a reduced assessment load** in the week before the 1 Nov and 1 Dec university deadlines (Guide p.13).

## Curving and grade boundaries

Attainments are **not recorded as raw marks** (Guide pp.11–12):

- Curved against **CIE past-paper data**, "allowing for where students are on their learning trajectory."
- **More generous in G10, stricter in G11** and later in the year.
- Grades "reflect your learning trajectory, not what you would score on a CIE exam today."
- Past-paper grade thresholds are "the best starting point" for setting boundaries.
- **Moderation** applies where an attainment runs across multiple classes taught by different teachers; the Head of Department checks large between-class differences and may adjust curves or boundaries.
- *"You will always be told how grade boundaries and curves are decided."*

An attainment "should make a reliable **Forecast Grade**" (Guide p.11).

## Grade conversion (Guide p.11)

| CIE scale | A-Level grade | BNDS GPA |
|---|---|---|
| 90–100 | A* | 4.3 |
| 80–89 | A | 4.0 |
| 70–79 | B | 3.5 |
| 60–69 | C | 3.0 |
| 50–59 | D | 2.5 |
| 40–49 | E | 2.0 |
| below 40 | U | 0 |

**Failing is below 50%** (Guide p.15). **At or below 70%** triggers the Academic Concern Steps — your advisor and the A-Level Director are informed and support measures follow (Guide p.13).

## Retake policy (Guide §IV, pp.15–16)

You get one opportunity to retake a failed course, in the holiday after the semester, with 2–3 teacher meetings for support. The work is "just as challenging" and similar in quantity to the original. The grading policy is explained before finals and **cannot be changed once agreed**. A signed academic-honesty declaration is required; plagiarism means immediate failure with no resubmission.

**A passed retake earns the equivalent of a D**, not the grade actually achieved. A failed retake leaves the original grade standing. Under force majeure, more than 50% completion plus written parent-signed evidence can pass; without evidence, fail.

Graduating seniors get only **two weeks** for a retake, because their Summer Holiday starts early.

classes/a-level-art-design/9479-departme.body:
# 9479 Department Handbook

Your Art & Design handbook covers the visual elements, the principles of design, the three components, the assessment objectives with checklists, the four disciplines, theme selection, artist studies, the Personal Study, and portfolio samples.

## Some numbers in it are from an older specification

The handbook was written for the earlier 9479 specification, not the one this cohort sits. **Do not rely on the sheet counts, hours, word counts or mark totals printed in it.** Use the current syllabus for those. The teaching content, prose and structure are still fine — this is only a numbers problem.

| Feature | Handbook says (old spec) | Use instead | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 name | "Component 1: Coursework" | Component 1: Portfolio (*coursework* is still a correct informal name) | p.34 |
| C1 mark | single mark out of 100 | mark grids | p.34 |
| C2 submission | three sheets of A2, photographed and mounted | all-digital submission | p.35 |
| C1 submission | five sheets of A2 | — | p.34 |
| C3 submission | eight sheets of A2 | — | p.37 |
| C3 written analysis | 1000–1500 words | **2000–2500 words** ← use this | pp.36, 104 |
| C3 mark | out of 100, "weighted to 200" | — | p.37 |
| AOs | AO1 Record · AO2 Explore · AO3 Develop · AO4 Present, flat weighting | new per-component splits | p.39 |

The handbook gives the C2 timed test as 15 hours (p.35); the correct duration will be confirmed in class.

The [[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|course page]] also warns against taking numbers from the older support documents.

## Things in the handbook that disagree with themselves

1. **Personal Study word count.** pp.36 and 104 say 1000–1500 words; pp.114–115 say 2000–3000 words and "should not exceed 3000 words." Ignore both — use **2000–2500 words** from the syllabus.
2. **Tint.** p.18 is correct: *tone* is adding darker shades, *tint* is adding white. The p.19 sub-glossary is wrong where it says "tint — Another word for shade."
3. **AO names.** Three different sets appear (pp.39, 72, 84). Treat p.39 as the correct one: Record / Explore / Develop / Present.

## What is in it

### Visual Elements (pp.7–23)

Six elements, each a definition plus a full-bleed plate: **Line** (Fred Sandback), **Shape** (Escher, *Sky and Water II*), **Space** (Doug Wheeler), **Tone** (Wolfgang Mattheuer), **Color** (pp.18–21, with a CMYK note and six example plates), **Texture**.

Form is not covered in this chapter. The fullest element vocabulary — including Form, with adjective banks for all six — is at **p.81** in the Artist Studies chapter, e.g. Texture: "flat, raised, smooth, rough, coarse, shiny, glossy, reflective, scratched, matt, satin, frosted, visible, smooth, blended, impasto, washes, glazes, stippled, splattered, bold, timid, lively, layered."

### Principles of Design (pp.24–30)

- **p.25 "How to Read Images"** — the four-stage method (Description · Formal Analysis · Interpretation · Judgement) over a grid of 15 paired opposites for visual communication: balanced/unstable · gestural/technical · sharp/diffuse · symmetry/asymmetry · active/still · distorted/realistic · solitary/juxtaposed · flatness/depth · transparent/opaque · regular/irregular · subtle/amplified · vivid/neutral · unified/fragmented · ordered/loose · light/dark
- **p.26 "17 Key Principles of Design"** — Alignment · Hierarchy · Contrast · Repetition · Proximity · Balance · Color · Space · Emphasis · Proportion · Rhythm · Pattern · Movement · Variety · Unity · Lines · Shapes
- **pp.27–30** — worked demonstrations of eight: Emphasis (focal point), Hierarchy, Scale/Proportion (size · ratio · divisions), Contrast (in shape · color · scale · layout), Repetition, Unity & Variety, Balance (symmetrical · asymmetrical)

### The four disciplines (pp.48–57)

**Fine Art** (painting, drawing, sculpture, photography, printmaking, mixed media, assemblage) · **Graphic Communication** (illustration, printmaking, packaging, branding, advertising, signage, typography) · **Three-Dimensional Design** (sculpture, ceramics, product, architecture, interior, environmental, set design, jewellery) · **Textiles and Fashion** (fashion design/illustration, costume, constructed textiles, screen printing, batik, digital-printed textiles, surface pattern).

You may focus on one discipline or combine several. Two distinctions:

- **Fine Art responds to a theme only**; the other three respond to a theme **or a brief** (pp.50–57).
- **3-D Design uniquely requires** you to consider "the setting in which the final outcome will be situated, e.g. interior/exterior, urban/rural" (p.55).

### Themes (pp.66–72)

Guidance on *choosing* a theme (this is Component 1-facing, p.66). Nine qualities of an appropriate theme (personal relevance · breadth and depth · creativity and originality · flexibility · researchability · visual and conceptual interest · educational value · relevance to the assessment objectives · engagement with broader issues), a seven-step selection guide, then the assignment: complete a theme selection form for at least four possible themes with related artists and possible artworks, choose one, and justify it. Submitted by the end of the week.

### Assessment Objectives (pp.38–47)

Take the assessment objectives and all rubrics from the current syllabus, not from this handbook. The handbook's AO **checklists (pp.41–47)** are still useful as scaffolding — for example, AO1's runs seven questions from "collected images to show your inspiration and stimuli?" through "clearly linked all of your work to your starting point?" — as long as the objectives they hang off come from the syllabus.

### Personal Study (pp.104–118)

Three study types (p.105), which can be combined:
- **Technical** — media, surfaces, tools, techniques
- **Stylistic** — signs, symbols, metaphor, meaning, figurative and formal elements
- **Contextual** — art and society; social, historical and cultural contexts; theories of art

The integration rule (p.105): *"the study will form the starting point of your practical coursework. The two must link together and inform each other i.e. they are not separate elements but dependent on each other. Your success depends on this point."*

Use the 2000–2500 word count from the syllabus, not the figures printed in this chapter.

### Portfolio samples (pp.119–205)

Around 87 pages of sample work, captioned ("Final Outcome", "SAMPLE 1 / Component 1").

## AI use

The examples in [[shared/bnds-ai-policy|the school AI policy]] are Art & Design examples, and its attribution requirements align with what the current syllabus asks for on AI-generated images.

classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-pl.body:
# PAL S1 Lesson 08: The Theme Shoot and the Contact-Sheet Edit

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-2-photography|Unit 2]] · U2·L3 · ← [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-07-light-shadow-and-the-series-theme|L07]] | [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-09-a2-the-photographic-series|L09]] →

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Session | W9, one Wednesday double (~90 min) |
| Date | Wed 2026-10-28 |
| Focus | The main theme shoot, then the contact-sheet edit — "shoot many, keep few, know why" |
| Deliverable | ≥20 new theme frames; a contact sheet with 12 selects and 6–8 series candidates marked |
| Feeds | **CS2 is collected this session** (composition set + contact-sheet edit); everything feeds A2 next week |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Shoot to a hard quota of at least 20 frames on your approved theme
2. Read a contact sheet: see everything small and together, keep few, write why
3. Edit in the honest order: crop, then tone, then color, and never on the only copy

## Goal

This session works the unit's two muscles back to back: **abundance** (a focused half-double shoot with a hard quota) and then **selection** (the contact-sheet ritual — see everything small and together, keep few, write why). Editing enters here too, in its honest order: crop first, then tone, then color — and never on the only copy.

## How it runs

- **Warm-up (5 min)** — theme pulse-check: state your theme and frame count so far. If you are stuck or without a theme, re-theme now from your L07 shortlist.
- **The theme shoot (35 min)** — on campus, solo, on your theme: **minimum 20 new frames.** The discipline rule: every frame states **one composition decision and one light decision** (thirds or broken? high or low? side-light or back-light?). Ask yourself for each frame: "what am I deciding here?"
- **Teach: the edit (15 min)** — back in the room. The contact sheet: why editors look at everything small, together, before choosing. Then the edit order — the same in **Photoshop, Affinity, or any editing platform**, phone editors included: **crop and straighten first → exposure and contrast → color last → work non-destructively** (adjustment layers in Photoshop/Affinity; on a phone, duplicate then edit — the original always survives). File hygiene in one line: your pictures are files; know where they live.
- **The contact-sheet edit (25 min)** — assemble all your theme frames (last week's homework + today's shoot) into a contact sheet — a Bridge/Lightroom contact sheet, the gallery grid screenshotted into the sketchbook, or printed strips. **Circle 12 keepers, then mark 6–8 series candidates.** Each cut gets a reason; each keep gets a reason. This, plus your L06 circuit frames, is **CS2 — collected before the close.**
- **Close (10 min)** — homework: finish the edits on your candidates (crop → tone → color, originals kept) and draft a sequence order for next week's A2 session.

2. Shoot one subject from five viewpoints and select three with written reasons
3. Apply the rule of thirds, and say when breaking it was deliberate

## Goal

The unit's motto is **"shoot many, keep few, know why."** You arrive with twenty photographs of one subject. The interesting decisions happen *before* the shutter — where you stood, what you put in the frame, what you left out — and choosing three from twenty is a skill with reasons, not a vibe.

## How it runs

- **Warm-up (10 min)** — cameras out: **any camera counts — phone, compact, DSLR** — and turn the framing grid **on** (grid overlay on phones, viewfinder grid on cameras; this is a standing habit for the unit). - **Teach (15 min)** — framing and viewpoint from the *Seeing Photographs* exemplars: **rule of thirds**, balance (symmetrical vs asymmetrical), horizon placement and tilt, **vantage point**, figure–ground. Each concept is one image and one question ("what did the photographer decide here?").
- **Viewpoint circuit (30 min)** — one subject per pair, five stations: **eye level · high · low · close · far-with-context**. Minimum fifteen frames each. The subject never moves; only the photographer does — viewpoint alone changes the picture's meaning.

## Focus

This lesson has two halves with one join. First: light has *direction and quality*, and moving yourself (or the lamp) is a decision as expressive as framing. ## How it runs

Exemplars from the shared library's Photographers collection — **Ueda's project folders, Hara's series, Atget's Versailles, Johansson's towns** — plus Cartier-Bresson's decisive moment from §4. Then the **A2 brief**: 6–8 photographs on one theme, selected from many, sequenced, titled, with a short reflection — made over the next two weeks, submitted in class W10.

## Objectives

1. Select and sequence 6–8 images so that removing any one costs the series something
2. Reject an off-theme frame even when it is the prettiest one

## Goal

You make A2 in this room, from work you have already done — the double is selection, sequence, and words, not new shooting. The test of a series: take any one image away — does the group lose something? Add your prettiest off-theme frame — does the group get worse? If you can answer both, you understand what you made.

## How it runs

- **Set-up (5 min)** — the criteria are on the board: **framing · viewpoint · light · series thinking.** Have all your frames, contact sheet, and edits open. From here it is your own pictures and your own reasons.

Two forced passes: the **kill-your-darlings pass** (your strongest image that doesn't serve the theme goes — into your sketchbook, with a note, not the series) and the **weakest-link pass** (if one image needed defending for two sentences, replace or cut it).

# PAL S1 Lesson 10: Juxtaposition and Scale

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Session | W11, one Wednesday double (~90 min) — Unit 3 opens |
| Dates | Wed 2026-11-11 |
| Focus | What collage is; juxtaposition and scale — "two images say a third thing" |
| Deliverable | Vocabulary in the sketchbook; two fast cut-and-paste studies (one juxtaposition, one scale) |
| Feeds | The experiment set that CS3 checks (W13) starts today |
| Homework | Collect raw material — old magazines, printed photos (including your own U2 frames), packaging, tickets; ≥20 usable images by next week; MB posting |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Say what juxtaposition does: two images together say a third thing
2. Use the wrong scale on purpose and say what it changes
3. Make two fast studies, one of juxtaposition and one of scale, and name the meaning each produces

## Goal

In Unit 2 you chose images; now you cut them apart and make them argue. The unit's spine is **combine · meaning** — a collage is not decoration, it is a sentence built from stolen words. Today sets up the two cheapest tools for meaning: **juxtaposition** (two things that don't belong together, together) and **scale** (the wrong size, on purpose).

## How it runs

- **Warm-up (10 min)** — the word itself: *coller*, "to glue." Four terms, written in your sketchbook: **collage** (glued combination of found/made images), **papier collé** (glued paper shapes), **photomontage** (collage made from photographs), **assemblage** (collage gone 3D).
- **The lecture (20 min)** — a brisk arc: Picasso and Braque glue newspaper into paintings (1912) → **Hannah Höch** cuts up Weimar Germany (Dada photomontage) → Matisse cuts pure color → Moholy-Nagy and **Rodchenko** build photomontage posters → contemporary digital collage. One question per stop: *what did gluing let them say that painting couldn't?*
- **Teach: the two tools (10 min)** — juxtaposition: the *Picasso-and-Höch* diptych side by side — same era, opposite temperaments. Scale: a teacup taller than a building means something; a person smaller than a shoe means something else. The rule: **a collage decision is a meaning decision.**
- **Studio: first cuts (35 min)** — two fast A5 studies from the shared material bin, working with scissors only today: (1) a **juxtaposition study** — two images that have no business together, one new meaning; (2) a **scale study** — one element deliberately the wrong size. Glue only after a dry-fit. Title each with one line: "this says …"
- **Close (15 min)** — table walk-through: your partner names the *third thing* your two images say — if they can't, the juxtaposition is decoration, not meaning yet. Studies into the sketchbook; homework brief (the material harvest).

## Materials and safety

Scissors only this session (knives enter at L11 with the safety brief): scissors, glue sticks, A5/A4 cartridge, the class material bin (pre-stocked magazines + printed images). Start collecting your own material today — a collage is only as good as its harvest.

## Assessment

Nothing graded today; both studies open the **experiment set** that CS3 checks at W13. Register: [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|PAL S1 Assessments]].

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Session | W12, one Wednesday double (~90 min) |
| Date | Wed 2026-11-18 |
| Focus | Layering (order, edges, transparency) and text as image — the unit's making session |
| Deliverable | A layering study and a text-and-image study added to your experiment set |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Order layers deliberately, so that what is in front is what wins
2. Choose between a torn and a cut edge, and say why that edge
3. Use text as a shape with a voice rather than as a caption

## Goal

Two craft skills separate a collage from a scrapbook page. **Layering**: what is in front is what wins — order, overlap, and edges (torn vs cut) are all decisions. **Text as image**: a word in a collage is not a caption, it is a shape with a voice — cut letters, headlines, and instructions carry tone before they carry information. Every exemplar today uses both at once.

## How it runs

- **Warm-up (5 min)** — last week's studies on tables; thirty-second recall: what was your third thing?
- **Teach: layering (15 min)** — three decisions demonstrated live as the dry-fit builds up: **order** (background first, the "speaker" last), **edges** (torn edge = soft/organic, knife edge = hard/mechanical — tear one, cut one, compare), **transparency** (tissue, tracing paper, thin magazine stock let layers talk). Exemplars: **Barbara Kruger** (text barking over found photographs) and **John Stezaker** (two images spliced so cleanly they become one wrong thing).
- **Blade safety + materials (10 min)** — craft knives enter here: cut away from the hand, blade shallow, cutting mat always, cap when walking, one knife per table returned to the tin. Materials tour: adhesives (glue stick for paper, PVA thin-spread for card), surfaces (cartridge vs card), the tissue/tracing drawer.
- **Studio: two studies (40 min)** — added to your experiment set: (1) a **layering study** — minimum three layers, at least one torn edge and one knife edge, one semi-transparent layer; (2) a **text-and-image study** — one found image + cut-out text that *changes what the image means* (not describes it). Dry-fit, photograph the dry-fit, then glue.
- **Close (10 min)** — pairs swap text studies and read them aloud in the voice the text suggests — if the reading voice is obvious, the tone worked. Reminder: CS3 collects the whole experiment set next Wednesday.

## The digital option

Editing platforms are Photoshop, Affinity, or any editor. You may **remix an analog study digitally** as an extra experiment, using layers, masking, and drawn interventions. Whether the *final* A3 can be digital will be confirmed in class.

## Assessment

## Goal

The final layer goes down and the collage starts speaking for itself. Ask one last time before you submit: *cover any one element — does the collage lose part of its sentence? If a piece is only decoration, it comes off.* A3 is a made-in-class attainment: the mark rewards decisions you can point to, in the work and in the reflection.

## How it runs

- **Set-up (5 min)** — work out, finishing lists out, criteria on the board: **juxtaposition · layering · composition · meaning.** From here: your board, your scraps, your reasons.
- **Studio (55 min)** — the finishing list, in order: the speaker placed and glued; text set last; edges resolved (every torn edge on purpose, every cut edge clean); the back signed with title and date. If you are working digitally, export your final and print or submit the file with the layered working version.
- **Reflection (15 min)** — one page, full sentences. Frames you can use: "My collage is about … " / "The juxtaposition of … and … says … " / "My layering decision that works best is … because … " / "I placed … at … so that … " / "If I made it again I would …."
- **Submit and close (15 min)** — submit your collage + reflection; put your process trail into the sketchbook: both drafts, the dry-fit photographs, and the best rejected scraps, annotated. Next Wednesday the course turns to **communicating to an audience** — graphic design and the poster, or the linocut route — and the A4 route is announced then.

## Assessment

**Full brief** (objectives, task, instructions, rubric): [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-a3-final-collage|A3 Collage]].

**A3 — final collage + reflection**, sat and submitted in class. Marking focus: **juxtaposition, layering, composition, meaning** — meaning is judged on the work *and* the reflection's reasons. Returned with feedback within five working days. Register: [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|PAL S1 Assessments]].

# PAL S1 Lesson 17: The Portfolio and the Sketchbook

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-4-graphic-design-and-the-poster|Unit 4]] · U4·L3 · ← [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-16-a4-the-final-poster|L16]] · **semester close**

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Session | W19, one Wednesday double (~90 min) — the semester's last teaching session, back from the break |
| Dates | Wed 2027-01-06 |
| Focus | Documentation; the End-of-Term portfolio assembled and submitted; **A5: the sketchbook submitted** |
| Deliverable | The EoT portfolio (one organized file) and the sketchbook, both handed in at close |
| Feeds | EoT (20%) and A5 (the fifth attainment) — the semester's final grades; the survey feeds next semester's shape |
| Homework | None — the semester's work is in. Return session Wed 2027-01-20: work back, grades, 1:1 feedback |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Select and sequence a semester of work into one organized portfolio
2. Submit the sketchbook as evidence of process across the semester (A5)
3. Say what the portfolio argues about your development, not only what is in it

## Goal

The semester ends the way every unit did: by choosing. Four finals, a term of process, forty-plus sketchbook pages — this double is for turning that pile into **one organized portfolio that argues you can see**, and for handing over the book that proves how you got there. Selection and sequence, one last time, at semester scale.

## How it runs

- **Set-up (5 min)** — everything out: the four finals (drawing, series, collage, poster), process work, sketchbooks. The submission checklist from the portfolio spec goes on the board.
- **Teach: what a portfolio argues (10 min)** — a portfolio is not a folder, it is a claim with evidence: **4–5 strongest works**, each with self-chosen supporting material (intention, reflections, sketches, tests, process photos — no single required formula), in **one clearly organized PDF or slide file**. An album page from eighteenth-century Japan makes the point: a collection, sequenced, reads as one argument. Choose what represents you, not what took longest.
- **Studio: document and assemble (50 min)** — photograph or scan anything not yet digital (flat, even light, square-on — the image-quality rules from the spec); select; sequence (strongest first and last, the L09 rule at term scale); one line of intention per work; export as one file, named properly. **Submit before the close.**
- **A5: the sketchbook (15 min)** — final pages settled, name on the spine, a paper slip marking the page you're proudest of. Books are collected: the fifth attainment, marked on **ideas, experimentation, visual research, reflection, presentation**.
- **Close (10 min)** — the **End of Semester Survey**: themes you'd want next semester, formats, freedom, what worked, the dream project. Ten quiet minutes. Last words: exam week next Wednesday (no class); everything returns **Wed 2027-01-20** with grades and 1:1 feedback.

## Assessment

**Full briefs** (objectives, task, instructions, rubric): [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-a5-sketchbook|A5 Sketchbook]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-eot-semester-portfolio|EoT Portfolio]].

**EoT — the semester portfolio (20%)**, submitted in session and reviewed during the exam window (no sitting). **A5 — the sketchbook**, the whole semester's book, submitted alongside it. Both are marked to the published criteria; grades and comments land at the return session, Wed 2027-01-20. Register: [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|PAL S1 Assessments]].

# PAL S1 Lesson 16: A4 — The Final Poster

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-4-graphic-design-and-the-poster|Unit 4]] · U4·L2 · ← [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-15-the-poster-message-audience-hierarchy|L15]] | [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-17-the-portfolio-and-the-sketchbook|L17]] →

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Session | W17, one Wednesday double (~90 min) — the last teaching session before the winter break |
| Dates | Wed 2026-12-23 |
| Focus | **A4 sat**: the final poster made in class, handmade or digital, plus the reflection |
| Deliverable | The final poster + reflection, submitted at close; thumbnails and type studies in the sketchbook as process |
| Feeds | A4 is the semester's fourth attainment; the work returns as portfolio material at W19 |
| Homework | Over the break: keep the sketchbook alive (2–3 pages a week — **A5 collects it on Jan 6**); read the portfolio spec; MB posting |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Execute your chosen thumbnail as a finished poster, handmade or digital
2. Deliver one message to one audience within the unit's three seconds and three meters
3. Write a reflection naming the hierarchy decisions you made

## What you do

You make one poster in one double, built from a thumbnail you already decided. The ninety minutes are execution with judgment. The standard is the unit's own test: pin it up, walk back three meters, count three seconds. If the message doesn't land in that window, no amount of craft saves it.

## How it runs

- **Set-up (5 min)** — criteria on the board: **hierarchy · typography · message · audience.** Bring your circled thumbnails; use paper and pens or the lab machines, whichever route you declared.
- **Studio (65 min)** — the build, with two standing checks. At **20 minutes**, the squint test — pin up or zoom out, stand three meters back, and ask what reads first. If it isn't the message, fix hierarchy before finishing anything. At **45 minutes**, the type pass — the title in its final voice, secondary text smaller than feels polite. **Text sets last.** If you are working digitally, save the layered working file; if you are working by hand, photograph the near-final state.
- **Reflection (10 min)** — one page. You can use these frames: "My poster is for [audience] and says [message]" / "The first thing you read is … because I … " / "My type sounds … because … " / "If it hung in the hallway I would change …."
- **Submit and close (10 min)** — submit your poster + reflection; put your process (all four thumbnails, type studies) into the sketchbook. Housekeeping: **no class the next two Wednesdays** (winter break 12-24 → 01-03); **Wed 2027-01-06 is the last session** — the EoT portfolio and the **A5 sketchbook** are both due that day. The portfolio spec goes home today.

## Assessment

**Full brief** (objectives, task, instructions, rubric): [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-a4-final-poster|A4 Poster]].

**A4 — final poster + reflection**, sat and submitted in class. Marking focus: **hierarchy, typography, message, audience**. Returned with feedback within five working days.

If your class is following the printmaking route, this session is instead the carve-ink-print double and **A4 is the final linocut** — same date, same focus in its own form (see the [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-u4-printmaking-variant|variant]]). Your teacher will confirm which route your class is taking in class.

Register: [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|PAL S1 Assessments]].

# PAL S1 Lesson 15: The Poster — Message, Audience, Hierarchy

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-4-graphic-design-and-the-poster|Unit 4]] · U4·L1 · ← [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-14-a3-the-final-collage|L14]] | [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-16-a4-the-final-poster|L16]] →

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Session | W16, one Wednesday double (~90 min) — Unit 4 opens |
| Dates | Wed 2026-12-16 |
| Focus | What a poster must do: message, audience, hierarchy, type as voice; thumbnails for the final |
| Deliverable | **CS4**: one annotated poster analysis + a four-thumbnail set with type studies, one circled with a reason |
| Feeds | A4 (you sit it next Wednesday, Wed 2026-12-23) |
| Homework | Gather or make anything your circled thumbnail needs (images, lettering references, files); MB posting |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Ask a poster its four questions: what does it say, who is it for, what reads first, what does the type sound like
2. Produce one annotated poster analysis (CS4)
3. Design four thumbnails with type studies and circle one with a reason

## Goal

Every unit this semester made images that could wait to be understood. A poster cannot wait: it has **three seconds and three meters** to deliver one message to one audience, or it has failed. Today compresses the whole discipline into its four questions — *what does it say? who is it for? what reads first? what does the type sound like?* — and ends with the final poster designed in thumbnail.

## How it runs

- **Warm-up (10 min)** — A3 collages returned with feedback; one written action each. Then the unit question, cold: *a poster in the hallway — what decides whether anyone reads it?*
- **Teach: the four questions (20 min)** — worked on exemplars, one question at a time. **Message**: one sentence or it isn't one. **Audience**: Mucha selling cherry-blossom calendars to Parisians; a print made cheap to travel to thousands (the Ukiyo-e argument from the printmaking deck). **Hierarchy**: the 1860s Gsell advertisement — one name card commanding a hundred small photographs; first read, second read, third read. **Type as voice**: the same word in three letterings sounds like three people — L11's text-as-image, now in charge.
- **Studio 1: the analysis (20 min)** — CS4 part one: take one poster from the spread (printed exemplars + the classroom deck), annotate it against the four questions, and state the first/second/third read with arrows. Plain sentences beat design words.
- **Studio 2: thumbnails and type (30 min)** — CS4 part two. The task: **a poster for an exhibition of your own work** — your A2 photo series or your A3 collage — for a real audience (this school, this hallway). Draw four thumbnails of the same poster with four different hierarchies (image-led, type-led, split, crowded-to-sparse); hand-letter the title word in two voices. **Circle one thumbnail, one line why.**
- **Close (10 min)** — **CS4 collected** (analysis + thumbnails + type studies).

## Assessment

**CS4 — thumbnail set + poster analysis** — is sat and collected in this double (focus: hierarchy and audience), one week ahead of the sitting it rehearses. **A4** — the final poster, handmade or digital, made in class next Wednesday (Wed 2026-12-23), marked on **hierarchy, typography, message, audience** — is announced today, with a week's notice. Bring what your thumbnail needs. Register: [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|PAL S1 Assessments]].

# 9607 Resource Library

## The coursebook

Marshall, Naisbett & Stoklosa, *Cambridge International AS & A Level Media Studies Coursebook*, CUP (©2016/2023, Cambridge-endorsed, ISBN 978-1-009-26224-8). It has eight units:

| Unit | Book pages |
|---|---|
| 1 Introduction to Media | 2–15 |
| 2 Media Language: Micro elements | 16–58 |
| 3 Media Language: Macro elements | 59–82 |
| 4 Textual Analysis | 83–104 |
| 5 Media Contexts | 105–136 |
| 6 Media Production: AS and A Level portfolios | 137–180 |
| 7 Media Debates | 181–221 |
| 8 Media Ecology | 222–252 |

The book defines terms inline; there is no glossary and no index.

## Past papers

Past papers are available for June 2024 and June 2025, covering Components 2 and 4 only. Components 1 and 3 are coursework.

**Paper 2** (Section A extract analysis and Section B contexts essay, 25 marks each): Section A asks you to analyse how the extract constructs meaning through camera, sound, mise-en-scène, and editing. You get four screenings, and the rubric allows 30/45/45 minutes.

**Paper 4** (A Level): Section A is three 15-mark essays from a fixed three-topic menu in order — regulation, postmodern media, power. Section B is a compulsory Media Ecology synoptic 30-marker.

Command words across all papers: Analyse / Explain / Evaluate / Assess / To what extent.

## How the papers are marked

**Paper 2** (each 25-mark section): five criteria, each marked independently on a 0–5 band, best-fit (a script can sit at different levels on different criteria):

| AO | Criterion | Marks |
|---|---|---|
| AO1 (15) | Media Concepts (language & representation) | /5 |
| AO1 | Contexts & Critical Debates (social significances) | /5 |
| AO1 | Use of Terminology | /5 |
| AO2 (10) | Analysis of how meaning is created, incl. use of theory | /5 |
| AO2 | Use of Examples | /5 |

Per-criterion band words: **5** Sophisticated / Insightful · **4** Thorough / Effective · **3** Clear / appropriate · **2** Limited · **1** Basic · **0** no creditable content. Paper 2 is weighted AO1 60 / AO2 40.

**Paper 4:** Section A's three 15-mark essays each use the same five criteria at 3 marks apiece; Section B's Media Ecology 30-marker uses generic level descriptors (Higher = Levels 4–5, Middle = Level 3, Basic = Levels 1–2). AO1 60 / AO2 40 overall.

This banding is used to mark A1, A4 and the EoT.
