# Oxbridge W03: Can Measurement Reach the Thing Itself?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2: The Gap]] · Week 3 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|← W02]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is the gap between us and the world a problem with our instruments, or a condition of being an observer at all? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | **None.** This session runs entirely on examples you already have. |
| Carried out | A tree falls in a forest with no one there. Does it make a sound? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Build an argument from examples you already have, with no reading to lean on
2. Say whether the gap between observer and world is an instrument problem or a condition of observing at all
3. Name what an instrument changes by measuring

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> A thermometer placed in a glass of water changes the temperature of the water.

Write silently for two minutes: is this a serious problem or a trivial one?

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

- Name a measurement that does not disturb what it measures.
- The double slit experiment: observing which slit the particle passes through changes the result. Is that the same kind of problem as the thermometer, or a different one?

Some things to test as you argue: if you calculate the disturbance and subtract it, you need another measurement, which also disturbs — does this ever terminate? If the effect only matters at very small scales, is the gap a fact about reality or a fact about magnitude?

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

Move the same problem into language.

- You say the water is cold. I say it is cool. Which of us is wrong?
- Some words cannot be translated. Does that mean the thing they name does not exist for other speakers, or only that it is harder to reach?
- Which gap is wider: between "cold" and the actual temperature, or between the thermometer reading and the actual temperature?

Both language and measurement involve a gap. Science narrows it. Nothing closes it.

Follow-ups: if the gap can be narrowed but never closed, is narrowing it progress *toward* something, or just narrowing? What would it feel like to have no gap — can you describe that state without using a representation?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

Is the gap a fact about our instruments, or a fact about reality? Choose one.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> A tree falls in a forest with no one there. Does it make a sound?

Bring an answer next week. [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] opens by polling it.

## Links

[[concepts/the-gap]] · [[concepts/the-ontological-turn]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]]

# Oxbridge W02: Do Images Represent Reality or Produce It?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1: The Image]] · Week 2 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|← W01]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is the quality of an image a technical fact or a political one? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/hito-steyerl\|Steyerl]], "In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux |
| Prepare | The single sentence in Steyerl you found **most arguable**, ready to say which and why |
| Bring | Two versions of one image: high resolution, and badly compressed / screen-recorded / re-uploaded |
| Carry out | A thermometer measures temperature. Does it show you the temperature, or change it? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Argue whether the quality of an image is a technical fact or a political one
2. Use Steyerl's poor image to make a case an opponent has to answer
3. Hold the distinction between representing reality and producing it without collapsing one into the other

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

Both versions of the image are on screen.

> Which of these is more real?

Two minutes of silent writing.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

Which one did you choose, and what does "more real" mean in your answer?

Questions to work through:
- More information **about what**? Is a blurry photograph of a real event less real than a sharp photograph of a staged one?
- If you chose the poor image because it has been seen more, has travelled — **why does travelling matter**?
- If the two produce different feelings, different levels of trust, and different audiences, in what sense are they the same image?
- Where did each of these images come from, and **who paid for the difference**? Does a high resolution image cost something a poor image does not?

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

Steyerl's central reversal:

> Resolution is not only a technical property. It is a marker of value, of institutional access, and of who is permitted to circulate. **The poor image is degraded because it moved. The high resolution image is pristine because it was kept.**

Questions:
- If an image loses quality every time it is shared, what does high quality tell us about how much it was shared?
- Steyerl says the poor image is about defiance and appropriation as much as about conformism and exploitation. Can something be both?
- Does an image represent an event, or does it produce the event **as a public thing**?
- Compression is measurable physics — so why do measurable properties map so cleanly onto ownership and institutional access?
- Is a poor image democratic, or only cheaper to distribute? Are those the same?
- Does this apply only to digital images, or also to prints, copies, textbook plates, museum lighting?
- Is a screenshot of a painting a painting? If an event is not photographed, did it happen publicly?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

Do images show us the world, or make the world showable? One sentence, one reason.

Back to week 1: if you said perception can be trained toward neutrality, say what a neutral image would look like **and who would be able to afford it**. See [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]].

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> A thermometer measures temperature. Does it show you the temperature, or change it?

This carries directly into [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]]. It may seem like a different subject. It is not.

## Links

[[entities/hito-steyerl]] · [[concepts/the-poor-image]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]]

classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-wr.body:
# Oxbridge Assessment — none

This course is not graded. There is no register of marks.

## What replaces marking

Nothing is measured, but there is still a standard for what a good contribution looks like, and it is named aloud in the room. A strong contribution shows:

1. **Commitment.** You take a position rather than survey positions.
2. **Pressure.** You name the strongest objection to your own case.
3. **Precision.** Your claim is narrow enough to be wrong.
4. **Movement.** The argument arrives somewhere it did not start.

You get these as spoken feedback in the commit movement — "that is a survey, not a position" is something you can act on immediately. They map onto the three interview moves: commitment is *take a position quickly*, pressure is *absorb the push*, and movement is what the mock debrief measures. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]].

## What the course tests

The course tests your speaking: fourteen commit movements, in which neutrality is the one banned position.

## The hedging repair

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]] is a pure pressure workshop — paired push practice and a four-line spine built in the room — and the same work happens in every session's commit movement.

## Discussion questions

The following prompts run as discussion questions, all in [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|the question bank]]:

- Is a low quality image worth less than a high quality one?
- Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or simply the condition of having a mind?
- Take one framework you rely on daily and show where it hides its own edges.
- Is forgetting a failure of memory or a function of it?
- Who decides what is visible, and does knowing the answer change anything?
- Is a view from nowhere possible?

classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w.body:
# Oxbridge W01: Is Perception Ever Neutral?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1: The Image]] · Week 1 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is seeing something we do, or something that happens to us? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/john-berger\|Berger]], *Ways of Seeing*, ch. 1, first six pages (the BBC episode of the same name is a second way in if the prose is hard) |
| Carried out | If seeing is never neutral, what is a photograph evidence of? |

## What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson you can:

1. Separate what you see from what you know from what you assume, on an unfamiliar image
2. State why seeing might be something that happens to you rather than something you do
3. Carry the question out of the room: if seeing is never neutral, what is a photograph evidence of?

## Before class

Read Berger, first six pages. If the prose is difficult, the BBC episode of the same name works as a second entry point.

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

You are shown an image you are not likely to recognize. After two minutes of silence, you write, in order:

1. What you **see**.
2. What you **know**.
3. Whether knowing changed the seeing.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

You describe what you saw. Where two people describe the same image differently, you look at why: is one of them seeing wrongly, and is there a description everyone would agree on?

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

You are told what the image is: title, date, context, and one further fact. You look again and ask: has the image changed, or have you?

Berger's claim then goes on the board: *the way we see things is affected by what we know or what we believe.* You test it — Berger says we never look at one thing, we look at the relation between things and ourselves. Is that true of a photograph of a stranger? Can you unlearn something in order to see freshly?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

**Is perception ever neutral?** You take a side in one sentence. Everyone answers.

Two positions to expect:

- **Trained eye** — perception is shaped, but training can make it more accurate, more neutral. (Better by what standard?)
- **No exit** — there is no neutral position to be trained toward. (If no view is better, why study anything?)

> [!note] Your answer is used again in Week 2.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> If seeing is never neutral, what is a photograph evidence of?

## Links

[[entities/john-berger]] · [[concepts/framework]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]]

# Oxbridge W04: Is There a Reality Behind Appearances?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2: The Gap]] · Week 4 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|← W03]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Last week asked how well we can know things. This week asks what kind of things there are to know |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/plato\|Plato]], Allegory of the Cave, *Republic* VII — clean modern translation, ≈ two pages |
| Bring | A Renaissance perspective construction |
| Carried out | Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or just the condition? **Bring a case** |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. State Plato's cave precisely enough to argue against it
2. Distinguish a question about how well we know things from a question about what kinds of things there are
3. Bring a case to the next session rather than a position

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

The question from last week is on the board:

> A tree falls in a forest with no one there. Does it make a sound?

We begin with a quick poll.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

If you said no: what exactly is missing when there is no one there?

Positions we will name and test:

- "The vibration happens, the sound does not, because sound requires a hearer."
- "Of course it makes a sound, physics does not need an audience."
- "It depends what you mean by sound." — If so, give both definitions and say which is doing more work.

Follow-up: Is this an argument about the world or an argument about a word? How would you tell the difference?

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

### Plato

Questions we will work through:

- The prisoners mistake shadows for real things. Is our situation the same as theirs, or different? Does knowing you are in a cave change your relationship to it, or only your feelings about it?
- You have never seen a perfect circle, only approximately circular things. But you know what a perfect circle is. Where does that knowledge come from? If it comes from averaging imperfect ones, how do you average toward a perfection you have never encountered?
- Is the prisoner who leaves better off than the ones who stay, or worse off because he cannot go back? This is Plato's own worry.

### Linear perspective

We look at a Renaissance perspective construction alongside Steyerl's argument from W02.

Questions:

- Perspective does not show us the world. It shows us the world from a point. What is the difference?
- If a perspective becomes invisible as a perspective, what do we think we are looking at?
- Is perspective a discovery about vision, or an invention that trained vision?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

Is there a reality behind appearances, and if there is, what would count as evidence of it?

> [!note] The trap
> The second half of that question is the trap. Any evidence arrives as an appearance.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> We cannot measure without disturbing. We cannot see without a position. Is that a loss, a liberation, or just the condition?
>
> **Bring a case.**

## Links

[[entities/plato]] · [[concepts/linear-perspective]] · [[concepts/the-ontological-turn]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]]

# Oxbridge W07: Argument Workshop

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3: Frameworks and History]] · Week 7 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|← W06]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Purpose | The midpoint. No new material — six weeks of discussion put under interview pressure |
| Duration | 45 minutes, in three movements: *what an argument is* / *live pressure* / *build the spine* |
| Reading | none |
| Carried question | Every framework so far turned out to hide its edges. Is there anything that does not? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Say what an argument is, as distinct from an opinion or a reaction
2. Hold a position under live interview pressure without either collapsing or digging in
3. Build the spine of an argument from six weeks of discussion, with no new material

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> Write the strongest objection to something you argued in the last six weeks.

Silent, two minutes. Object to yourself, not to a classmate.

## Movement 1 · what an argument is (10 minutes)

Two paragraphs go on the board, both about the same topic. One surveys three views and concludes that the truth lies somewhere in between. One takes a narrow position and names the case that would defeat it.

**Questions.**

- Which of these could be wrong? Which could be right?
- Which one would you rather have to defend? Which one is worth listening to?

**The principle.**

> An argument is not a survey of views. It is a committed act of reasoning. A claim narrow enough to be wrong is worth more than a claim broad enough to be safe.

The paragraphs are specimens to judge, not models to imitate — nothing in this course is written for submission ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]). The difference between surveying and committing is easier to see laid out than to hear.

## Movement 2 · live pressure (15 minutes)

Pairs. One student states a position in one sentence. The partner pushes three times using only these moves:

1. **The consequence.** If that is true, then what follows?
2. **The hard case.** Here is an example your claim does not cover.
3. **The definition.** You used a word that is doing all the work. Define it.

Swap. Then debrief on one question only:

> At which push did you stop thinking and start defending?

This is the same question the mock interview debrief asks. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]].

## Movement 3 · build the spine (10 minutes)

Produce, on paper, four lines. This is a scaffold for speaking, not a submission — it stays with you and nothing is collected.

1. My claim, in one sentence.
2. The reason.
3. The strongest objection.
4. Why the claim survives, or how it must narrow.

Three are read aloud, and the group attacks them.

Four lines is also the shape of a good interview answer under pressure: claim, reason, the objection you volunteer before it is put to you, and what you concede. If you can produce it on paper in ten minutes, you can produce it aloud in ninety seconds.

## Closing (5 minutes)

> Every framework so far turned out to hide its edges. Is there anything that does not?

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]] · [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|Assessment — none]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]]

# Oxbridge W06: Does Reality Have a History?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3: Frameworks and History]] · Week 6 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|← W05]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Things considered real in the past are now considered false. Does this mean we were wrong then, or that reality itself changed? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | none |
| Bring | **Three artifacts** — Mercator beside Gall-Peters; an early modern map showing Taprobana; a one-paragraph account of Barry Marshall, 1984 |
| Carried through | The Merleau-Ponty quotation: the body is our general medium for having a world. If that is true, what happens when the medium is wrong? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Say whether a superseded belief means we were wrong then, or that reality itself changed
2. Use a historical example precisely rather than as illustration
3. Hold a position on whether reality is the kind of thing that can have a history

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> Name one thing people used to be certain about that we now consider false.

Two minutes, silent, one example each.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

Examples are collected and sorted into two columns: things that were *factually wrong*, and things where the *category itself* has shifted.

**Questions.**

- Were the people who believed these things stupid, or were they reasoning well from a different starting point?
- **Which of your examples will our grandchildren put on this list about us?**

| Point raised | Follow-up |
|---|---|
| "They just did not have the data" | **Barry Marshall.** The data was available; the framework rejected it. What does a framework do to data it cannot accept? |
| "Some of these are not facts, they are definitions" | Which ones, and why is the line hard to draw? |

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

### The map

Mercator beside Gall-Peters.

**Questions.** Is Mercator a lie? What is it good at? Who benefits from what it is good at? **Is a projection that distorts nothing possible?**

| Point raised | Follow-up |
|---|---|
| "Not a lie, it is useful for navigation" | So a framework is **a set of chosen sacrifices** — which sacrifices are visible to the user, and which are not? |
| "Every map distorts, so it does not matter" | Does every distortion have the **same consequences**? |

### Taprobana

An island appeared on maps for centuries, referring unstably to Sri Lanka, to Sumatra, to nowhere. Sailors sailed toward it. **Question.** Was Taprobana real? What would it take to answer that?

### The video game map

**Question.** In a game, the edge of the map is disguised as a feature of the world. The mountain is too high. The road is closed. **Why disguise it instead of showing a wall?**

The answer: because a visible wall reminds you that you are inside something.

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

[[entities/roland-barthes|Barthes]]:

> The author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all.

**The insight.** A biased history book is not the problem. The problem is the one that claims not to be. The framework hides its limits by making them look like the world.

**Question.** Name one framework you use every day that claims not to be one. Every student answers — examples include exam grades, the calendar, the news feed, "common sense", the school timetable, the map app. W07 puts these claims under pressure, so you leave with a claim of your own to defend.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> The body is our general medium for having a world. If that is true, what happens when the medium is wrong?
>
> — Merleau-Ponty, *Phenomenology of Perception*, 1945

## Links

[[entities/roland-barthes]] · [[concepts/naturalization]] · [[concepts/framework]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]]

# Oxbridge W11: Whose Agreement Makes a Thing Real?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6: Collective Reality]] · Week 11 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|← W10]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Some things are real whether or not anyone agrees. Some things are real only because everyone agrees. Where is the line, and who draws it? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | none |
| Bring | The ten-item list, on the board |
| Carried into next week | Can we still share one world, or only private ones? |

## What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Draw the line between what is real regardless of agreement and what is real only because of it
2. Say who does the agreeing, on a case like money, borders or weekends
3. Defend the placement of a hard case on either side of that line

## Opening (5 minutes)

Ten items are on the board. You sort them into two columns, silently, for two minutes.

> gravity · money · a nation · Tuesday · a species · a debt · a disease · a genre · a race · a language

## Movement 1 (10 minutes)

Start with the easy ones, then work through the hard cases:

- **A species:** is the boundary in nature or in the classification?
- **A disease:** was it there before it was named? Was addiction a disease in 1850?
- **A race:** what happens to your sorting here, and why is it the hardest one?

## Movement 2 (15 minutes)

The political turn:

- Does agreement require **everyone**, or **enough people**, or **the right people**?
- Name something that was real by agreement and stopped being real. What did the ending look like?
- If a hundred people agree and one refuses, **is the one wrong, or outside?**
- Whose disagreement counts as disagreement, and whose counts as error?

## Movement 3 (10 minutes)

Name one thing you believe is real that most people around you do not, and say what would make it count. This forces you to describe the **mechanism** of realness rather than just assert an instance of it.

## Closing (5 minutes)

> Can we still share one world, or only private ones?

## Links

[[concepts/framework]] · [[concepts/the-ontological-turn]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12]]

# Oxbridge W08: Can the Body Be Trusted?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4: The Body and the Machine]] · Week 8 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|← W07]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | You know you are cold because you feel it. Is feeling more reliable than any system, or is the body just another framework? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | **None.** One quotation sent in advance |
| Sent ahead | "The body is our general medium for having a world" — [[entities/maurice-merleau-ponty\|Merleau-Ponty]] |
| Carried out | What can you do that a machine cannot? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Argue whether feeling is more reliable than any system, or whether the body is another framework
2. Test one quotation against your own experience rather than restating it
3. Carry out the question of what you can do that a machine cannot

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> Describe being cold without using the word cold, and without using a number.

Two minutes, silent.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

- Can you be wrong about being cold?
- If a thermometer says 22 degrees and you are shivering, **which one is wrong?**

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

Four cases, introduced one at a time.

| Case | The question |
|---|---|
| **Phantom limb** | A person feels pain in a leg that is not there. Is the pain real? Is it accurate? |
| **Chronic pain without injury** | The signal fires with nothing to report. Is the body lying, or reporting honestly about itself? |
| **Synaesthesia** | Someone hears color. Are they perceiving more of the world, or differently? |
| **Adaptation** | Move from a cold room to a warm one and the same water feels hot, then neutral. **Which reading was correct?** |

Questions:

- Is the body a window onto the world, or a medium that shapes what can appear in it?
- Merleau-Ponty says the body is the medium for having a world. If the medium is wrong, **are you wrong about the world, or do you have a different world?**
- Is a blind person perceiving less of the world, or a different world?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

The Spinoza reframe:

> We do not yet know what a body can do.

Stop asking what a body **is** and ask what a body **can do**. Does that dissolve the problem or dodge it?

State a position: the body is an instrument to be corrected, **or** the body is the condition of there being anything to correct.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> What can you do that a machine cannot?

## Links

[[entities/maurice-merleau-ponty]] · [[entities/friedrich-nietzsche]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]]

# Oxbridge W13: Who Gets to Show Us the World?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7: Power and Visibility]] · Week 13 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|← W12]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is being seen a form of recognition or a form of capture? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | Two short extracts: [[entities/michel-foucault\|Foucault]] on the panopticon (*Discipline and Punish*); [[entities/frantz-fanon\|Fanon]], the look passage (*Black Skin, White Masks*) |
| Carried forward | Is a view from nowhere possible? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Argue whether being seen is recognition or capture
2. Set Foucault's panopticon against Fanon's look and say what each one catches that the other misses
3. Name who holds the position of showing, and who is required to be seen

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> Describe a situation in which being watched changed what you did, even though nobody said anything.

Two minutes, silent.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

Questions to discuss:

- Did you change because you **were** watched, or because you **might be** watched?
- Is there a difference between being **watched** and being **seen**?

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

### Foucault

The panopticon works because the prisoner cannot tell when he is watched, so **he watches himself**. Power becomes automatic and no longer needs an operator.

Questions:

- If power works best when nobody has to exercise it, **where is it located**?
- Is visibility a trap? **Who set it?**
- Is a framework that makes you police yourself more or less powerful than one that punishes you?

### Fanon

The look does not merely observe. **It fixes.** It arrives before you speak and decides in advance what you are.

Questions:

- Foucault says visibility is a trap. Fanon says invisibility is also one. **Can both be true?**
- Is demanding to be seen a demand for power or a request for permission?
- Who in this room has the option of being unmarked, of being seen as simply a person rather than as a type?
- Who can afford invisibility, and who is punished by it?
- Does being represented give you the position of **the one who shows**, or only of the one shown?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

One line to hold the whole course together:

> **Every framework has a maker, and the maker is not in the picture.**

Question: Does knowing who made the frame change anything, or only how you feel about it? If you think awareness is enough, say enough for what.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> Is a view from nowhere possible?

## Links

[[entities/michel-foucault]] · [[entities/frantz-fanon]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]

# Oxbridge W12: Is a Common World Still Possible?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6: Collective Reality]] · Week 12 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|← W11]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | If each of us is served a different version of the world, is a shared world still available, and would it have to be built without representation? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, **Movement 2 is student-led** |
| Reading | [[entities/irmgard-emmelhainz\|Emmelhainz]], "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", e-flux |
| Prepare | The **angle sheet**: one central question, eight angle questions. Pick one and bring a position |
| Leads to | Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Say what follows if each person is served a different version of the world
2. Use Emmelhainz to ask whether a shared world would have to be built without representation
3. Argue for or against the possibility of a common world, and name the cost of your answer

## Preparation

There is one central question the whole discussion builds toward, and eight smaller questions beneath it approaching the same problem from different directions. Pick one angle. You do not need a final answer, just a position you are willing to defend and have challenged.

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> Compare your feed with the person next to you. How much overlap is there?

Two minutes. Then: **is that a difference of taste or a difference of world?**

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

**Questions.**

- What is the last thing you can be **certain** everyone in this room saw?
- Is a shared world a shared set of facts, a shared set of images, or a shared set of problems?

| You might say | Consider |
|---|---|
| "We all live in the same physical world, so there is no problem" | Does that shared physical world help you agree about **anything you actually disagree about**? |
| "It has always been like this, people always had different information" | Is a difference of degree becoming a difference of kind — **and how would you tell**? |

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes) — student-led

You present your chosen angles, one at a time, **each answering a single question from the room before the next speaks.** The angles are clustered on the board as they arrive.

**Questions to run through the presentations.**

- Emmelhainz asks whether we can share a world **beyond** representation. What would that even be? **Give one example of something shared that is not represented.**
- Is the problem too many representations, or the fact that representation was always the wrong medium for sharing a world?
- If a common world has to be **made** rather than found, who is making it now?
- Is agreeing to disagree a shared world, or the end of one?

| You might say | Consider |
|---|---|
| "Shared experience, not shared images: eating together, working together" | **Does that scale beyond a room?** |
| "We should just fix the algorithms" | Fix them **toward what**? Someone chooses the target, which returns us to W11 |

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

**Question.** Is a common world still possible? If yes, **name the ground it stands on**. If no, say what replaces it.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?

## Links

[[entities/irmgard-emmelhainz]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]]

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-prep.body:
# Oxbridge Interview Preparation

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus

## What the interview actually tests

**Not knowledge.** This course is built on one claim:

> The Oxbridge interview tests whether a candidate can think while being watched, revise a position without collapsing, and stay with a difficult question rather than resolving it prematurely.

The whole seminar prepares you for that, but three moves are practiced explicitly.

## The three moves

**1. Take a position quickly.** Candidates who hedge lose the interview in the first minute. State a claim, then qualify it. **Never qualify first.**

**2. Absorb the push without abandoning the claim.** When the interviewer objects, respond with neither surrender nor repetition. Use one of two sentences:

> "That case is harder for my position, and here is why I think it still holds"
>
> "That case actually defeats my position, so let me narrow it."

**3. Follow the consequence.** The interviewer is usually asking where your claim leads, not whether it is true. **Volunteer the consequence before being asked.**

## The push line format

Every question in [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|the question bank]] has two parts: a plain opening question, and a push line replicating the interviewer's follow-up move. Practice them in pairs, with one student as interviewer.

> **Opening.** Is a photograph evidence?
>
> **Push.** You said it depends on whether it was edited. Every photograph involves choices about framing, exposure, and moment. So is every photograph edited, and does your distinction survive that?

## Mock interview format

**Twelve minutes per student. One question, no preparation time.**

The interviewer's job is to **push three times, not to be fair.**

Debrief for three minutes afterward on one thing only:

> At which push did the candidate stop thinking and start defending?

## Where the moves get drilled inside the course

The three moves are not confined to mock interviews. Each has a home session:

- **Take a position quickly** — Movement 3 of every session. One sentence, one reason, no abstentions. [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template|The template]] bans neutrality precisely to train this.
- **Absorb the push** — [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]] runs it as a paired drill with the three named pushes (the consequence, the hard case, the definition), and debriefs on the same question the mock does. W07 is entirely this drill, which makes it the most direct interview rehearsal in the fourteen weeks.
- **Follow the consequence** — [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|principle 5]]: the teacher asks about the consequence inside your own claim all term, so you hear the move roughly forty times before you have to perform it.
- **Movement under argument is praised, not penalized.** [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] makes changing position under pressure an explicit skill: anyone who moves columns must name the quotation that moved them.

## Scheduling

Mock interviews run in the week following [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]. That week is not one of the fourteen. At twelve minutes plus a three-minute debrief per student, a full round is roughly 15 minutes each, so a single 45-minute session covers three students. The exact number of sessions will be confirmed in class.

## The connection to the closing session

W14's whole purpose is the capacity the interview is testing:

> The best outcome is a room that can hold the paradox without either collapsing into relativism or fleeing back to naive realism. That capacity, holding a genuinely open question without needing to close it, is precisely what an Oxbridge interviewer is testing for.

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-.body:
# Oxbridge Course Design Principles

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]]

Six rules shape each session: how it is built, how questions are worded, and what a good session looks like.

## 1. The question does the work

The teacher does not deliver a position. A question draws one out of you. In a well-run session, you and your classmates do the arguing and the teacher mostly redirects.

## 2. Build from what you already know

Sessions never open with a philosopher. They open with something you can already answer from experience: a map, a thermometer, a feeling of cold, a video-game boundary, a photograph on a phone. The philosopher arrives later, only to **name** what you have already been arguing.

You will see this in every session:

- Berger goes on the board in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]] only after you have generated the idea yourselves.
- Barthes arrives at the *end* of [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], to name what you built out of maps and video-game boundaries.
- Spinoza's reframe closes [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]] rather than opening it.

## 3. Questions are plain on the surface, catalytic underneath

The questions are written as single plain lines:

- "What does the world look like?"
- "Where does the body end?"
- "Who agreed that this is real?"

There are no sub-questions or explanations attached to the question itself. The complication comes in the live follow-up, not on the slide. This is why [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|the question bank]] is written as single lines.

## 4. Close with a defensible position, not a summary

Every session ends by asking you to state a position you are willing to defend under pressure. That closing question is carried out of the room, not resolved in it.

## 5. Complication comes from inside your own claim

The Socratic move is not to bring in a counterexample from outside. It is to find the consequence you have not yet noticed inside your own claim, and to ask about that.

For example:

> "You said the body cannot lie. What about phantom limb pain?" is weaker than "You said the body cannot lie. Does that mean a person who feels pain in a missing leg is feeling something true?"

Both use the same case. The second makes your own claim do the work.

## 6. Register

Sentences are short and vocabulary is plain. **Difficulty lives in the idea, never in the syntax.** A hard concept in easy words is the target. This is why the course can run Foucault, Bergson and Emmelhainz with Grade 11 ESL students without dilution — the concepts are not simplified, the sentences are.

## How the principles show up elsewhere

- The five-part session shape in [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template|the template]] makes principles 1 and 4 structural: two minutes of silent writing so you enter with something of your own, and a commit movement where neutrality is the one banned position.
- [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]] turns principle 5 into a drill — you perform the push line yourself instead of the teacher.
- The four qualities the course names — commitment, pressure, precision, movement — are principle 4 stated as feedback. Nothing is graded ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|Assessment — none]]), so these are said aloud in the commit movement rather than written down: "that is a survey, not a position" is a sentence you can act on immediately.

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list.m.body:
# Oxbridge Reading List

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus

Everything the fourteen sessions read, quote, show or cite.

## Set texts, assigned

| Week | Text |
|---|---|
| W01 | John Berger, *Ways of Seeing*, ch. 1 — first six pages |
| W02 | Hito Steyerl, "In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux journal |
| W04 | Plato, Allegory of the Cave, *Republic* VII — a clean modern translation, roughly two pages |
| W09 | Tobias Rees, on AI and the concepts of the modern period, Noema |
| W12 | Irmgard Emmelhainz, "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", e-flux journal |
| W13 | Michel Foucault, *Discipline and Punish* — panopticon extract |
| W13 | Frantz Fanon, *Black Skin, White Masks* — the look passage |

For W01, the BBC episode of *Ways of Seeing* is a second way in if you find the prose difficult.

## Quotations used live

Five quotations are delivered on the board rather than read in advance:

- **Merleau-Ponty**, *Phenomenology of Perception*, 1945 — the body as general medium for having a world. (W08; sent in advance)
- **Sartre** — man is condemned to be free. (W05)
- **Camus** — the absurd as confrontation between human need and the silence of the world; we must imagine Sisyphus happy. (W05)
- **Barthes** — the author who disappears behind the text. (W06)
- **Spinoza** — we do not yet know what a body can do. (W08)

## Extension reading

Offered to groups that want to keep going; none is assigned.

- Susan Sontag, "In Plato's Cave", from *On Photography*
- Amelia Groom, "Permanent Collection"
- Donna Haraway, "Situated Knowledges"
- Benjamin Bratton, *The Terraforming*, or the shorter Noema pieces
- Rebecca Solnit, on maps and atlases
- Henri Bergson, *Matter and Memory*, on habit memory and pure memory
- Sigmund Freud, on repression and the return of the repressed
- Guy Debord, *The Society of the Spectacle*
- Mark Fisher, *Capitalist Realism*
- Tim Ingold, *The Perception of the Environment*, introduction

Sontag's "In Plato's Cave" is also an assigned text in Art Appreciation, and Debord has an entity page from Media Studies ([[entities/guy-debord]]).

## Visual and material references

- Mercator projection beside Gall-Peters (W06)
- Early modern maps showing Taprobana (W06)
- Renaissance perspective constructions (W04)
- Carsten Höller, the laboratory of doubt — for the body sessions (W08, optional visual anchor)
- One image no student will recognize: a minor painting, an unlabelled photograph, an object in an unfamiliar context (W01) — plus one uncomfortable fact about it, withheld until Movement 2
- Two versions of one image, high resolution and badly compressed (W02)

## Cases used as examples

The course runs more on cases than on texts. The named ones:

- The thermometer, and the double slit experiment (W03)
- Barry Marshall and *H. pylori*, 1984 (W06)
- Taprobana, the island that appeared on maps for centuries, referring unstably to Sri Lanka, to Sumatra, to nowhere (W06)
- The video game map whose edge is disguised as a mountain (W06)
- Phantom limb, chronic pain, synaesthesia, thermal adaptation (W08)
- The painted sheet — remembering as repainting (W10)
- The ten-item sorting list: gravity, money, a nation, Tuesday, a species, a debt, a disease, a genre, a race, a language (W11)

W06 uses three artifacts brought to the room: the two map pairs and a one-paragraph account of Marshall.

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-struct.body:
# Oxbridge Session Structure Template

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus · **45 minutes**

Every session in the course follows the same shape. Once you know this page, you can follow any session quickly.

## The five parts

| Part | Minutes | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Silent opening | 5 | One question on the board. You write for two minutes. **No answers taken yet** |
| Movement 1 · elicit | 10 | Positions on the table. Concrete, experiential, no theory. The goal is disagreement, not accuracy |
| Movement 2 · complicate | 15 | The case, image or example that breaks the easy answer. The philosopher may arrive here |
| Movement 3 · commit | 10 | One sentence and one reason from every student. Others may challenge |
| Closing | 5 | One question on the board, unanswered, carried into next week |

### Silent opening

Two minutes of writing before anything is said. This guarantees you enter the session with something of your own, which matters especially for quieter and less confident speakers. In an ESL room this is not a warm-up; it is what makes the rest of the session possible.

### Movement 1 · elicit

Positions go on the table. When a disagreement appears, it is named out loud — "So we have two camps in the room." The goal is disagreement, not accuracy, so a wrong answer stated clearly is more useful here than a hedged correct one.

### Movement 2 · complicate

The case, image or example that breaks the easy answer. Pressure comes **from inside your positions rather than against them** (see [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|principle 5]]). This is where a thinker may arrive, "and only to give a name to the position a student has already taken."

### Movement 3 · commit

Each student states a position in one sentence and gives one reason. Others may challenge.

> [!important] No neutral positions
> No student is allowed to remain neutral. Neutrality is the one banned position in this room.

### Closing

One question written on the board, unanswered, carried into the next week. It is posted to the group chat afterward with a quote attached.

## After the session

A short recap message goes to the group chat: two or three sentences naming what emerged, one quote for the next session, and the closing question restated. The register is casual.

This is the only routine outside the room. It keeps the closing question live across seven days, and it is where the next session's text or quotation is seeded.

## Where sessions deviate

Three of the fourteen sessions bend the template:

- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]]** — the movements become *what an argument is* / *live pressure in pairs* / *build the spine*. Consolidation, no new material.
- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12]]** — Movement 2 is student-led; each student presents a chosen angle and answers one question from the room before the next speaks.
- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]** — the template is dropped entirely for four questions at roughly ten minutes each, and there is no closing question. For the first time in fourteen weeks, you answer one instead.

classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-uni.body:
# Oxbridge Unit 1: The Image

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 1 of 8 · Weeks 1–2 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2 →]]

## Unit question

**Do images represent the world, or do they produce it?**

## What this unit is about

You already live inside images. You have opinions about resolution, screenshots, compression, filters, and what counts as a real photograph. This unit starts there: it needs no prior reading to enter and stays rigorous once you are in.

[[entities/john-berger]] gives the first idea: seeing is not neutral. [[entities/hito-steyerl]] turns that into a political and economic argument.

This unit also introduces the method you will use for the rest of the course: start from an intuition you already hold, test it against a single hard case, and then let a thinker name what you have been arguing. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|Course Design Principles]].

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01: Is perception ever neutral?]] — one unfamiliar image, seen twice: before and after being told what it is. Berger comes in only at the end.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02: Do images represent reality or produce it?]] — the same image at two resolutions. Steyerl turns the vocabulary of compression into an argument about access.

## Key texts

- [[entities/john-berger]], *Ways of Seeing*, chapter 1 (first six pages; the BBC episode is an alternative entry point)
- [[entities/hito-steyerl]], "In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux journal

See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/the-poor-image|The Poor Image]] · [[concepts/framework|Framework]]

## Preparation

Both sessions set a reading — the only consecutive pair in the course that does. Nothing is written or collected; the course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]. Come to W02 having read Steyerl, and pick the single sentence you found most arguable — be ready to say which and why.

## What you should leave with

> [!note] By the end of this unit
> A defensible position on whether image quality is a technical property or a political one, and the beginning of a suspicion that the way something is shown is doing more work than what is shown.

## Bridge to Unit 2

> [!note] Looking ahead
> If the image is not a neutral window, the next question is whether anything is. That moves the argument from pictures to measurement, where you might expect to find safety.

W02 closes on one line — *a thermometer measures temperature; does it show you the temperature, or change it?* [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]] removes the safety.

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank..body:
# Oxbridge Question Bank

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus

Single-line questions covering the full course arc — "plain on the surface, catalytic underneath." Use them as openers, as closing questions, or as interview prompts. The single-line form is deliberate: the printed question stays plain, and the complication comes in the spoken follow-up.

## Image and perception

- Is perception ever neutral?
- What is a photograph evidence of?
- Is a low quality image worth less than a high quality one?
- Do images show us the world or make the world showable?
- Is a screenshot of a painting a painting?

## Measurement and the gap

- Can measurement reach the thing itself?
- Is the gap a problem with our instruments or a condition of observing?
- Which is wider, the gap between "cold" and the temperature, or between the reading and the temperature?
- What would it feel like to have no gap?

## Appearance and reality

- Is there a reality behind appearances?
- Where does your idea of a perfect circle come from?
- Does knowing you are in a cave change your relationship to it?
- Is the prisoner who leaves better off than the ones who stay?
- Is perspective a discovery or an invention?

## The gap as a way of living

- Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or just the condition?
- Can you lose something that never existed?
- Is revolt a position or a mood?
- Must we imagine Sisyphus happy?

## History and frameworks

- Does reality have a history?
- Were we wrong then, or did reality change?
- Is a map that distorts nothing possible?
- Was Taprobana real?
- Name a framework you use every day that claims not to be one.
- Why does a game disguise its edge as a mountain?

## The body

- Can the body be trusted?
- Can you be wrong about being cold?
- If the thermometer says 22 and you are shivering, which is wrong?
- Is a blind person perceiving less of the world, or a different world?
- What can a body do?

## Human and machine

- What can you do that a machine cannot?
- Is the line between people and machines essential or contingent?
- Can there be understanding without life?
- What would a machine have to do for you to withdraw your answer?
- Could a machine have a past?

## Memory and forgetting

- What survives forgetting?
- Is forgetting a failure of memory or a function of it?
- Is a memory you revisit often more reliable or less?
- Are you responsible for what you forget?
- What is the difference between remembering and remembering remembering?

## Collective reality

- Whose agreement makes a thing real?
- Does agreement require everyone, enough people, or the right people?
- If a hundred agree and one refuses, is the one wrong or outside?
- Is a common world still possible?
- What is the last thing everyone in this room definitely saw?

## Power and visibility

- Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?
- Is being seen recognition or capture?
- Who can afford to be invisible?
- Is awareness of a framework enough, or does it change nothing?

## Synthesis

- Is a view from nowhere possible?
- What does the world look like?
- How does the world appear to us?
- Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework?
- What distinguishes a good frame from a bad one, if closeness to reality is unavailable?

## Interview format, with push lines

Practice in pairs. The push replicates the interviewer's follow-up move. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]] for the three moves being drilled.

**Is a photograph evidence?**
> Push: you said it depends on editing. Every photograph involves framing, exposure, and a chosen moment. So is every photograph edited, and does your distinction survive?

**Can a machine understand?**
> Push: you said understanding requires experience. Describe a test that would tell you whether another person has experience. If you cannot, is your criterion doing any work?

**Is a common world still possible?**
> Push: you said shared experience rather than shared images. Does that scale beyond a room, and if not, have you described a shared world or a small one?

**Were we wrong then, or did reality change?**
> Push: you said we were simply wrong. What counts as a disease has changed. Was addiction not a disease in 1850, or did we fail to notice that it was?

**Is being seen recognition or capture?**
> Push: you said the answer is to avoid visibility. Who has that option, and who is punished for taking it?

## How the bank maps onto the weeks

Each block belongs to a session, so you can use the bank for revision as well as for openers.

| Block | Session |
|---|---|
| Image and perception | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral\|W01]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it\|W02]] |
| Measurement and the gap | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself\|W03]] |
| Appearance and reality | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances\|W04]] |
| The gap as a way of living | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition\|W05]] |
| History and frameworks | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history\|W06]] |
| The body | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted\|W08]] |
| Human and machine | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent\|W09]] |
| Memory and forgetting | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting\|W10]] |
| Collective reality | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real\|W11]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible\|W12]] |
