classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-uni.body:
# Oxbridge Unit 3: Frameworks and History

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 3 of 8 · Weeks 6–7 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|← Unit 2]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4 →]]

## Unit question

**Does reality have a history?**

## The core question

Things considered real in the past are now considered false. Does that mean we were wrong then, or that reality itself changed?

You will work through three examples:

- **The Mercator projection**, beside Gall-Peters — not a lie, but a choice with consequences.
- **Taprobana**, an island that appeared on maps for centuries and referred to something, unstably. Sailors sailed toward it.
- **Barry Marshall**, who in 1984 had to infect himself because a framework in good standing could not accommodate the claim that ulcers were bacterial. Here the data was available and the framework rejected it.

## The key idea

> [!note] Key idea
> A biased history book is not the problem. The problem is the one that claims not to be.

Think of a video-game map: the edge is disguised as a feature of the world — the mountain is too high, the road is closed. A framework hides its own limits by [[concepts/naturalization|naturalizing]] them, because a visible wall would remind you that you are inside something.

At the end of W06, [[entities/roland-barthes]] names it: the author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06: Does reality have a history?]] — the three examples, the video-game map, and Barthes as the closing name.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07: Argument workshop]] — the midpoint. No new material; six weeks of discussion put under interview pressure, in pairs.

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/naturalization|Naturalization]] · [[concepts/framework|Framework]] (deepened — introduced in Unit 1, given its defining property here)

## Preparation

Neither session sets a reading. Both are discussion only ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]). In W07 you will produce four lines on paper, but they are an in-session scaffold for speaking, not a submission.

## The workshop drill

W07 puts under pressure the framework example you named in W06 — a framework you use every day that claims not to be one.

> [!important] The drill
> Hedging feels safe and polite, but in an Oxbridge interview it reads as having nothing to say. The rule is simple and worth repeating: **claim first, qualification second, never the reverse.**

## What to keep in mind

- The core question has no settled answer. "We were wrong then" preserves a stable reality and makes knowledge historical; "reality changed" makes reality historical, which is harder to hold but not absurd, since what counts as a disease, a species or a nation genuinely does change. The useful move is to ask what each answer costs.

## Bridge to Unit 4

You will look for something that stands outside history. The body is the obvious candidate: cold is cold in any century. W06 closes on the Merleau-Ponty quotation to set this up, and [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]] tests the candidate.

# Oxbridge Unit 2: The Gap

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 2 of 8 · Weeks 3–5 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|← Unit 1]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3 →]]

## Unit question

**Can any representation reach the thing itself?**

## The arc

Three sessions, each turning the same problem. This is the longest unit and the one that introduces the course's central term.

**Week 3, epistemology.** A thermometer changes the temperature of what it measures. Observation in the double slit experiment changes what is observed. Language calls something warm, and warm means different things to different speakers. You will likely conclude that the gap is wider in language than in science but present in both — that is the starting point, not the end.

**Week 4, ontology.** The question shifts from how well we can know things to what kind of things there are to know. [[entities/plato]] arrives here, alongside [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]] — a technique for depicting the world from a point that came to look like the world itself.

**Week 5, the existential turn.** Having established that the gap cannot be closed, you are asked how to live with it. [[entities/jean-paul-sartre]], [[entities/albert-camus]] and Heidegger are used as three positions you can adopt and defend.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03: Can measurement reach the thing itself?]] — the thermometer, the double slit, then the same problem moved into language. No reading.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04: Is there a reality behind appearances?]] — the cave and the perspective construction. The ontological turn.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05: Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or a condition?]] — four quotations, three columns on the board, and permission to change columns.

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/the-gap|The Gap]] · [[concepts/linear-perspective|Linear Perspective]] · [[concepts/the-ontological-turn|The Ontological Turn]]

## Preparation

Only W04 sets a reading (Plato, ≈ two pages). W03 and W05 run entirely on cases and quotations delivered live, so the reading load is lightest where the ideas are hardest.

What you carry between sessions is a position. W03 closes on the tree in the forest, with instructions not to discuss it before W04. W04 asks you to **bring a case** to W05. Nothing is written or collected — the course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]].

## What to expect

If you have a science background, you may treat science as the exception — the frame that gets closer to truth. Build that case as strongly as you can in Week 3. In Week 4 you will be asked what distinguishes a good frame from a bad one if closeness to an unframed reality is not available as a criterion.

- **W03:** the claim is not that measurement is unreliable — it is that measurement is an *interaction*, and an interaction has two sides. Precision and disturbance are not opposites; the more precisely you interact, the more you interact.
- **W05:** the existentialists are positions, not biography. The aim is to be able to say "I hold the Sartre position and here is why the Camus objection does not defeat it."

## Bridge to Unit 3

If frameworks cannot be escaped, the next question is whether they change — a historical question. W05 closes on it directly: *things considered real in the past are now considered false — were we wrong then, or did reality change?* This leads into [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3]].

# Oxbridge Unit 6: Collective Reality

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 6 of 8 · Weeks 11–12 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|← Unit 5]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7 →]]

## Unit question

**Whose agreement makes a thing real?**

## Week 11: agreement

Money is real, borders are real, weekends are real, and none of them would survive if everyone stopped agreeing.

The session runs on one exercise: sort ten items into *real independently* and *real by agreement* — **gravity, money, a nation, Tuesday, a species, a debt, a disease, a genre, a race, a language.** Gravity and Tuesday sort themselves; the hard ones are the point.

Then the harder version, which is the unit's actual subject: **agreement is never equally weighted. Whose agreement counts?**

In the final movement you name one thing you believe is real that most people around you do not, and say what would make it count.

## Week 12: Emmelhainz

[[entities/irmgard-emmelhainz]], "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", argues that the shared world has fragmented into private, algorithmically shaped worlds, and asks whether a common ground can be found that does not depend on representation at all. This is the most contemporary text in the course.

The session is structured differently from every other: one central question with eight angle questions beneath it, printed on a student sheet. Each student picks an angle, brings a position, and presents it — answering one question from the room before the next speaks. **Movement 2 is student-led.**

> [!note] Your framing for W12
> There is one central question the whole discussion builds toward, and eight smaller questions beneath it approaching the same problem from different directions. Pick one angle. You do not need a final answer, just a position you are willing to defend and have challenged.

The question is not whether the feed is bad, but whether **sharing a world** requires representation at all.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11: Whose agreement makes a thing real?]] — the sorting exercise, then the political turn.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12: Is a common world still possible?]] — Emmelhainz, and your own feeds as the opening evidence.

## Concepts introduced

None new. The unit is [[concepts/the-ontological-turn|the ontological turn]] applied collectively — realness as a relation rather than a property, now with the question of who holds the relation.

## Preparation

This unit carries the heaviest student preparation in the course, and it is all spoken.

- **W11:** nothing in advance.
- **W12:** read Emmelhainz, choose one of the eight angle questions, and arrive with a position on it. Movement 2 *is* the students, so come prepared.

Nothing is written or collected ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]).

## Bridge to Unit 7

If agreement is unequally weighted, the next question is who holds the weight — [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7]].

# Oxbridge Unit 7: Power and Visibility

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 7 of 8 · Week 13 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|← Unit 6]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8 →]]

## Unit question

**Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?**

## The two positions

**[[entities/michel-foucault]]:** visibility is a trap. The panopticon works because the prisoner does not know when he is watched, so he watches himself. Power does not need to look; it needs only to be *able* to look.

**[[entities/frantz-fanon]]:** being seen is not neutral either. The look can fix a person in place, arriving before they speak and deciding in advance what they are. Fanon adds what Foucault leaves out: **not everyone is seen the same way.**

## What this unit collects

This unit pulls together everything that came before. The framework that hides its edges is now revealed to have an owner. Perspective has a position, and someone occupies it. The map has a maker. The category has an author.

The line at the centre of this session is the course's whole argument compressed:

> **Every framework has a maker, and the maker is not in the picture.**

You re-read every earlier unit through it — [[concepts/linear-perspective|perspective]] from W04, the Mercator projection from W06, [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]] itself. Nothing new is introduced; what changes is that the frameworks acquire owners.

## Session

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13: Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?]] — two short extracts, and the awareness-versus-action question pressed hard.

## Concepts introduced

None new. The unit supplies the political reading of [[concepts/framework|framework]] and [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]] that the earlier weeks held back.

## Preparation

Read two short extracts, Foucault and Fanon. This is the densest reading in the course, so read closely — the session runs on discussion, not decoding.

Nothing is written or collected: the course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]. The session's central question is *who decides what is visible, and does knowing the answer change anything?*

## What to expect in discussion

- **Fanon is not an illustration of Foucault.** The point of putting them together is the asymmetry: Foucault describes a general condition, Fanon describes a distributed one. Not everyone is seen the same way, and a theory of visibility that cannot register that difference is exactly the kind of framework this course has been dismantling.
- **The awareness question.** "Does knowing who made the frame change anything, or only how you feel about it?" If you say awareness is enough, be ready to say **enough for what**. W14 will apply this same question to the course itself.
- **Two easy exits are closed.** "So the solution is not to be seen" meets *who can afford invisibility, and who is punished by it?* "Representation fixes this, more people on screen" meets W12: *does being represented give you the position of the one who shows, or only of the one shown?*
- **The opening prompt is personal and low-cost:** describe a situation in which being watched changed what you did, even though nobody said anything.

## Bridge to Unit 8

W13 closes on the course's title question, and the final move turns the critique back on the course itself. [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8]].

concepts/framework.md.body:
# Framework

**The [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]]'s central term**, and the subject of its throughline:

> Frameworks conceal their own constructed edges, and they actively shape reality rather than merely representing it.

A framework is **any system that makes something knowable by excluding most of what could be known.**

## Three properties

1. **It is a set of chosen sacrifices.** The Mercator projection preserves angles and distorts area. **There is no projection that sacrifices nothing.**
2. **It is productive, not merely descriptive.** [[concepts/linear-perspective|Linear perspective]] did not record how vision works. It trained vision to work that way.
3. **It hides its own edges.** This is the property the whole course turns on. See [[concepts/naturalization]].

Property 3 is what makes the term non-trivial. Everyone accepts that frameworks exist; the claim that does the work is that they **systematically conceal that they are frameworks.**

## Test question

> Name a framework you use every day that claims not to be one.

You answer this in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], where every student responds. Possible answers: exam grades, the calendar, the news feed, "common sense", the school timetable, the map app. Your answer becomes your essay topic in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]].

## Where the term gets its edges

The concept is built across the course rather than defined once:

| Session | What it adds |
|---|---|
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral\|W01]] | Seeing is already framed before any interpreting begins |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances\|W04]] | A framework can be a datable invention that comes to look like the world |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history\|W06]] | Property 1 (chosen sacrifices) and property 3 (hidden edges), via the map and the video-game boundary |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real\|W11]] | Frameworks are collectively held, and the holding is unequally weighted |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world\|W13]] | **Every framework has a maker, and the maker is not in the picture** |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible\|W14]] | The term is turned on itself: is "everything is a framework" a framework? |

## The self-application problem

The course's final question is whether the concept survives being applied to itself. Two live answers, both developed in [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]]: either the demand for an unframed view is incoherent rather than merely unsatisfied, or frames can be compared by their consequences without any access to an unframed reality — which is [[concepts/situated-knowledge|Haraway's route]].

## Related in other courses

Media Studies reaches the same territory through [[concepts/representation|representation]] and mediation — media do not show the world, they go between us and it, selecting and shaping on the way. The vocabulary differs; the claim about selection is the same one.

concepts/linear-perspective.md.body:
# Linear Perspective

Linear perspective is a datable invention that came to look like the structure of vision itself. It is a key example in the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]].

> Perspective does not show the world. It shows the world **from a point.** It assumes a single, motionless, monocular viewer, and it converts that assumption into geometry so convincing that for centuries it read as simply how things look.

## The philosophical payoff

When a perspective becomes **invisible as a perspective**, we mistake it for the world.

That is [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]] made visible. You can watch it happen rather than being told about it: here is the construction, here is the date, here is the assumption it encodes. Other cases of naturalization in the course (the map, the video-game boundary, the category) have to be argued for; this one can be demonstrated.

## A question to think about

> Is perspective a **discovery** about vision, or an **invention** that trained vision?

Follow-ups from [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]]: *perspective does not show us the world, it shows us the world from a point — what is the difference?* and *if a perspective becomes invisible as a perspective, what do we think we are looking at?*

## Where it comes from in the course

Not from art history. It arrives via [[entities/hito-steyerl|Steyerl]] in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]] and is developed in W04 alongside Plato — so you meet it as a claim about images and access before you meet it as a claim about vision.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[entities/hito-steyerl]] · [[concepts/framework]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] (in the list of frameworks that hid their edges)

## Materials

See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

concepts/naturalization.md.body:
# Naturalization

**The process by which a constructed thing comes to look like a natural fact.**

## Three images to remember

- **The video game map.** The edge is disguised as a feature of the world. The mountain is too high. The road is closed. **A visible wall would remind you that you are inside something.**
- **The history book that claims no bias.** A biased book is not the problem. The book that claims not to be is.
- **[[entities/roland-barthes|Barthes]].** The author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all.

## Why this concept and not just "framework"

Naturalization is the mechanism that makes [[concepts/framework|framework]] the central term rather than a trivial one. **Everyone accepts that frameworks exist. The claim that matters is that they systematically conceal that they are frameworks.**

Without naturalization, "everything is a framework" is a shrug. With it, the claim has a testable consequence: you should expect the most powerful frameworks to be the ones that feel least like choices.

## The demonstrable case

[[concepts/linear-perspective|Linear perspective]] is naturalization you can watch rather than be told about — a technique, invented at a datable moment, that came to read as the structure of vision itself.

## Where it is developed

In [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], you build the concept out of maps and video-game boundaries first; the Barthes line comes at the end to name what you have made.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]

W13 completes it: the naturalized framework turns out to have a maker, and **the maker is not in the picture.**

concepts/situated-knowledge.md.body:
# Situated Knowledge

**[[entities/donna-haraway|Donna Haraway]]'s answer to the choice between objectivity and relativism**, and a useful counter-move in the final weeks of the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]].

## The argument

The view from nowhere and the view from everywhere are **the same evasion**, because both refuse responsibility for a position.

Knowledge is always from somewhere, and admitting where does not weaken the claim. **It makes the claim accountable.**

## Why it matters

By week 13 you can see that two positions are both bad: "science is neutral" and "everything is subjective." Situated knowledge is a third option you can actually defend:

> A partial view that names its own location is better than a total view that does not — and **better is a real word here rather than a rhetorical one.**

That last clause is what makes the concept do work in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]. The session's first question asks what distinguishes a good frame from a bad one if closeness to an unframed reality is unavailable. Situated knowledge supplies a criterion — accountability of position — that does not require the unframed reality the course has spent fourteen weeks removing.

## The pressure it still faces

It does not dissolve W14's fourth question. If every position is situated, the claim that every position is situated is also situated, and the regress is the same one. What it changes is the consequence: on Haraway's account the regress is not a problem to be escaped but the reason for naming your location, which is a livable answer rather than a resolution. Whether that is enough is a genuinely open question.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] (as an extension) · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] · [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]]

## Reading

Haraway's "Situated Knowledges" is on the course's extension list, not assigned. The concept is taught from the argument rather than the text.

concepts/the-ontological-turn.md.body:
# The Ontological Turn

**The pivot from asking *how well can we know things* to asking *what kind of things are there to know*.**

The epistemological question assumes a stable reality and asks about the reliability of our access. The ontological question **suspends that assumption.**

## The classroom version

The tree falling in the forest.

> [!note] The key distinction
> Those who say there is no sound are not claiming that our hearing is unreliable. They are claiming that **sound is a relation rather than a property.**

That distinction is the entire concept. In [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] you meet the question without discussing it, and in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] you poll it. You will have taken a side without knowing which question you answered.

## Why the course needs it

> [!note] Why this matters
> This is the move that makes the second half of the course possible. Once reality is allowed to be relational, questions about history, the body, machines, and collective agreement all become live in the same way.

Each later unit is the same turn applied to a new domain:

| Unit | The relational claim |
|---|---|
| [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history\|U3]] | What counts as a disease or a species is historical, not fixed |
| [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine\|U4]] | Agency and understanding may be separable from being alive |
| [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality\|U6]] | Money, nations and debts are real by a relation, not a property |

## The test

W04's follow-up question:

> [!important] Ask yourself
> Is this an argument about the world or an argument about a word? **How would you tell the difference?**

If you cannot separate the two, you have made a semantic point and mistaken it for an ontological one — the most common failure mode of this concept.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11]] · [[entities/plato]]

concepts/the-gap.md.body:
# The Gap

**The distance between a representation and the thing represented, which can be narrowed but not closed.**

The organizing term of [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]] of the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]], and the concept the rest of the course argues from.

## Established in three moves

- **Measurement.** The thermometer changes the water. Observation changes the double slit result. **Measuring is an interaction, and interactions have two sides.**
- **Language.** Cold means different things to different speakers. Some words do not translate.
- **Perception.** Nothing reaches you except through a body that processes it.

## Beyond the first conclusion

A common conclusion is that science narrows the gap and language widens it. That is correct but insufficient. The real question follows:

> Is narrowing progress **toward** something, given that the target cannot be inspected?

That question turns an epistemological observation into [[concepts/the-ontological-turn|an ontological one]], and it is why [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] deliberately does not resolve.

## Three positions on it

These are not three answers to be graded, but three stances you can adopt and defend:

| Position | The claim | The pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **Loss** | There is a real world and we are locked out of it | Locked out implies you know what is on the other side. How? |
| **Liberation** | If there is no fixed reality, we get to make one | Make one out of what? |
| **Condition** | It is just what having a mind is like | If it is simply the condition, why does it feel like a loss to so many people? |

Worked in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] against Sartre, Camus and Heidegger. Heidegger's contribution threatens the term itself: if the framework is what makes understanding **possible** rather than what blocks it, does the word "gap" still fit? **Is a lens an obstacle to sight?**

## The point to hold

> The claim is not that measurement is unreliable. It is that measurement is an interaction, and an interaction has two sides. **Precision and disturbance are not opposites; the more precisely you interact, the more you interact.**

This is not the same as "everything is subjective." That reading makes the concept useless — it removes the difference between narrowing the gap and ignoring it.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]]

Applied to your own past in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]] — the painted sheet is the gap between a memory and its event.

entities/benjamin-bratton.md.body:
# Benjamin Bratton

**Born 1968.**

## The claim in one line

Computation is **planetary infrastructure** rather than a set of tools, and AI may be the only way to know systems too large for any single mind to perceive.

## Key quote

> The Copernican trauma was not that we were displaced, but that we could only know it through an instrument.

## How the course uses him

Bratton is the natural extension after [[entities/tobias-rees|Rees]] if you want to go further.

He reframes AI as **an instrument of perception rather than a rival to human thought** — which connects back to the thermometer in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]]. If knowing through an instrument is the normal condition rather than a compromise, the Week 9 question shifts: the interesting thing about a machine is not whether it thinks like us, but what it lets us see.

The quote above puts [[concepts/the-gap|the gap]] and the AI question in a single line.

## Reading

*The Terraforming*, or the shorter Noema pieces. This is extension reading, not assigned.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[entities/tobias-rees]]

concepts/the-poor-image.md.body:
# The Poor Image

**[[entities/hito-steyerl|Hito Steyerl]]'s term for the low-resolution, heavily compressed, repeatedly re-uploaded image.**

## The argument in one move

Resolution looks like a technical property but functions as a **marker of value, access, and institutional ownership.**

> An image degrades because it circulates. A pristine image is pristine because it was **kept** rather than shared.

The poor image is therefore simultaneously **evidence of exclusion and of defiance** — what remains when something travels far enough to reach people who were never the intended audience.

Steyerl uses vocabulary from science and computing — resolution, compression — and then turns it philosophically.

## Questions to consider

> Is a poor image democratic, or only cheaper to distribute? **Are those the same thing?**

If an image loses quality every time it is shared, what does high quality tell us about how much it was shared?

One claim to test: "They are the same image." If two versions produce different feelings, different levels of trust, and different audiences, **in what sense are they the same?** To hold this line, you have to argue that an image is its file rather than its effects — a defensible position, but a hard one.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]]

Steyerl's account of [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]] carries forward into [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]], so the two concepts arrive from the same source a fortnight apart.

## Also taught in Art Appreciation

The same Steyerl essay is an assigned text in Art Appreciation's [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-11-aura-and-the-poor-image|L11]], paired with Benjamin on aura. The Oxbridge course does not hold it — see [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]]. The two treatments differ: Art Appreciation runs a degradation lab (degrade an image on purpose, describe exactly what changed); Oxbridge runs it as an argument about who could afford a neutral image.

concepts/view-from-nowhere.md.body:
# View from Nowhere

**Thomas Nagel's phrase for the aspiration to a perspective that belongs to no particular position: complete, unlocated, unframed.**

The [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]] uses it as its closing question, and it names the course throughline in five words.

## Two live answers

**No, and the demand is a category error.** Asking for an unframed view is asking to see without being anywhere. That is not a failure we suffer — it is an incoherent request.

**No, but the aspiration still does work.** Frames can be compared even without access to an unframed reality: by their consequences, by what they let us do, by whose costs they hide. See [[concepts/situated-knowledge]].

The question is genuinely open, and the course does not pick.

## The final trap

> Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework? **If yes, why accept it. If no, you have just produced the view from nowhere.**

This is the fourth question in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] and the reason the session exists.

> [!note] Holding an open question
> The aim is to hold the paradox without either collapsing into relativism or fleeing back to naive realism. That capacity — holding a genuinely open question without needing to close it — is precisely what an Oxbridge interviewer is testing for.

## What the phrase collects

By W14 the term is doing retrospective work — every framework the course examined is an instance of a view **from somewhere** that presented itself as a view from nowhere:

the map · [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]] · the body as medium · machine cognition · the categories that decide who counts · and, if the fourth question lands, the course itself.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8]] · [[entities/friedrich-nietzsche]] (perspectivism as the counterweight when students try to rescue an unframed view) · [[entities/donna-haraway]]

## About the phrase

The phrase is borrowed from Nagel; the concept as taught is the course's own. If you go looking for Nagel's *The View from Nowhere* (1986), you will find an argument with a different shape.

entities/donna-haraway.md.body:
# Donna Haraway

**Born 1944.**

## The claim in one line

The view from nowhere and the view from everywhere are **the same evasion**; knowledge is always situated, and naming its position makes it **accountable** rather than weaker.

## Quote

> I am arguing for politics and epistemologies of location, positioning, and situating.

## Where she fits in the course

Haraway offers a third option when you get stuck between neutral science and total relativism. The course spends six weeks removing the neutral view and rules out the relativist shrug, so both of those are dead ends. [[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated knowledge]] is the way out that does not require taking either back.

She also extends naturally from [[entities/tobias-rees|Rees]] in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] if you want to keep going.

## Concept

[[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated Knowledge]] — the argument in full, and the pressure it still faces in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]'s fourth question.

## Reading

"Situated Knowledges" is on the extension list. It is not assigned. The concept is taught from the argument rather than the text. The essay is considerably harder than anything else the course assigns.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[concepts/situated-knowledge]] · [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]]

entities/frantz-fanon.md.body:
# Frantz Fanon

**1925 to 1961.**

## The claim in one line

The look does not merely observe; **it fixes** a person in place, arriving before they speak and deciding in advance what they are.

## Quote

> I was given not one but two, three places.

## How the course uses him

Fanon is paired with [[entities/michel-foucault|Foucault]] to introduce asymmetry:

> Foucault describes a general condition of visibility. Fanon describes a **distributed** one. A theory of visibility that cannot register **who is seen how** is exactly the kind of framework this course dismantles.

Questions to consider:

- Foucault says visibility is a trap. Fanon says invisibility is also one. **Can both be true?**
- Is demanding to be seen a demand for power, or a request for permission?
- **Who has the option of being unmarked** — of being seen as simply a person rather than as a type?

Both easy exits are closed. "The solution is not to be seen" meets *who can afford invisibility, and who is punished by it?* — and "more representation fixes it" meets *does being represented give you the position of the one who shows, or only of the one shown?*

## Set text

The passage from *Black Skin, White Masks* in which he is fixed by a look and a phrase before he has spoken. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]] · [[entities/michel-foucault]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7]]

entities/friedrich-nietzsche.md.body:
# Friedrich Nietzsche

**1844 to 1900.**

## The claim in one line

There are no facts, only interpretations, and **the demand for a disinterested view is itself an interested move.**

## Quote

> There is only a perspective seeing, only a perspective knowing.

## Where he appears in the course

He has no session of his own and no set text. He comes up in two places:

- As the strongest statement of the position [[concepts/view-from-nowhere|the closing question]] tests.
- In [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]], as the suspicion that **the body, not the mind, is doing the reasoning.**

## The risk

Nietzsche is easy to use as a conversation-ender ("there are no facts, so nothing you say counts"). Notice that move when it happens: perspectivism as a claim still has to be argued for, and if it is true of itself it is one perspective among others. That is the fourth question of [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] arriving early — which is fine, as long as you name it.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]] · [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]]

entities/henri-bergson.md.body:
# Henri Bergson

**1859 to 1941.**

## The claim in one line

Lived time is **duration** — accumulated and indivisible, not a sequence of separable states — and memory divides into **habit** performed by the body and **pure memory** that survives whole.

## Key quote

> The past survives under two distinct forms: in motor mechanisms, and in independent recollections.

## How this course uses him

Bergson appears in two places:

- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|Week 9]]** — he supplies the strongest objection to machine minds: **a system that can be reset to a previous state has no duration.**
- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|Week 10]]** — he reframes forgetting as a failure of *attention* rather than of *storage*. On this account we forget nothing; we simply cannot attend to most of it.

The two uses connect through a question raised in Week 10: if a machine forgot the way a body forgets, by accumulating distortion rather than deleting files, **would the week-9 objection survive?**

## Paired with Freud

Week 10 runs Bergson and [[entities/sigmund-freud]] as two incompatible accounts converging on one conclusion — **forgetting is a function of memory, not a failure of it.** They disagree about almost everything else, and that is the point: it is the course's cleanest example of an argument that does not depend on picking a winner.

## Reading

*Matter and Memory*, on habit memory and pure memory, is on the extension list. It is not assigned.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]] · [[entities/sigmund-freud]]

entities/irmgard-emmelhainz.md.body:
# Irmgard Emmelhainz

**Contemporary.**

## The claim in one line

The shared world has fragmented into **private, algorithmically shaped worlds**, which raises the question of whether a common ground can be found that does not depend on representation at all.

## The central question

> Can we share a world beyond representation?

This is her essay title and the session's central question.

## How the course uses her

She is the set text for week 12, and the most personally implicating reading in the course.

The question is philosophical, not a complaint about social media: not whether the feed is bad, but whether **sharing a world requires representation at all.**

If you answer "shared experience, not shared images — eating together, working together," that is the strongest available answer, and the question back is: **does that scale beyond a room?** If it does not, you have described a shared world or a small one, and saying which is the whole argument.

## Session format

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12]] is the only student-led session: one central question with eight angle questions beneath it, each student taking an angle and presenting a position.

## Set text

"Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", e-flux journal. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]]. Freely available.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6]]

entities/hito-steyerl.md.body:
# Hito Steyerl

**Born 1966.**

## The claim in one line

Image quality is not only a technical property; it is **a marker of value, access, and circulation** — and perspective shows the world from a point rather than showing the world.

## Quote

> The poor image is a copy in motion.

## In the Oxbridge course

Steyerl opens the first unit. She lets you use your own vocabulary of resolution and compression, then turns that vocabulary into a political argument.

Her account of [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]] carries forward into [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]], so her argument spans two units.

## Set text

"In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux journal. Write one paragraph on **the single sentence you found most arguable** before [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]]. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Concept

[[concepts/the-poor-image|The Poor Image]] — the term and its argument in full.

## Also taught in Art Appreciation

[[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-11-aura-and-the-poor-image|L11]] pairs her with Benjamin on aura and runs a degradation lab. In Oxbridge the same essay is an argument about who can afford a neutral image; in Art Appreciation it is an argument about what reproduction does to a work.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]] · [[concepts/the-poor-image]] · [[concepts/linear-perspective]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]]

entities/jean-paul-sartre.md.body:
# Jean-Paul Sartre

**1905 to 1980.**

## The claim in one line

There is no given human essence, so we are wholly responsible for what we make of ourselves — which is **a burden rather than a gift.**

## Quote

> Man is condemned to be free.

## His place in the course

Sartre is **one of three available positions on [[concepts/the-gap|the gap]].**

He answers the *loss* camp directly: **you cannot lose an original that never existed.** If you arrive at [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] saying "there is a real world and we are locked out of it," you meet the question: *can you lose something that never existed?*

**The word "condemned" is worth pushing on.** Why the harsh word, if freedom is good?

## What you need to be able to do

You do not need Sartre's biography. You need to be able to say "I hold the Sartre position and here is why the Camus objection does not defeat it."

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] · [[entities/albert-camus]] · [[concepts/the-gap]]

entities/maurice-merleau-ponty.md.body:
# Maurice Merleau-Ponty

**1908 to 1961.**

## The claim in one line

Perception is not a mental picture assembled from data; **the body is the medium through which there is a world for us at all.**

## Key quote

> The body is our general medium for having a world.

*Phenomenology of Perception*, 1945. You receive this reading before [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]].

## How the course uses him

He is the anchor of week 8. The question to follow up:

> If the body is the medium, **what happens when the medium is wrong?**

Phantom limb and chronic pain are the test cases; synaesthesia and thermal adaptation extend them. The sharpest form of the question, once the cases are on the table: *if the medium is wrong, are you wrong about the world, or do you have a different world?*

The quotation is also [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]]'s closing question, so it appears a week before the session that uses it.

## Where the session goes next

Merleau-Ponty establishes the body as medium rather than window; Spinoza's reframe closes the session by changing the question from what a body **is** to what a body **can do**. That shift makes [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] continuous with W08 — both map capacities instead of testing essences.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]]

entities/michel-foucault.md.body:
# Michel Foucault

**1926 to 1984.**

## The claim in one line

Power operates through **visibility and classification** rather than only through force; the panopticon works because the watched person, uncertain when they are seen, **watches themselves.**

## Quote

> Visibility is a trap.

## How the course uses him

**Week 13.** The central point is not to treat the panopticon as a simple metaphor for surveillance cameras, but to press the harder claim: **power that makes you police yourself needs no operator at all.**

Questions to carry it: *if power works best when nobody has to exercise it, where is it located?* · *is visibility a trap — who set it?* · *is a framework that makes you police yourself more or less powerful than one that punishes you?*

The opening prompt sets it up without naming him: describe a situation in which being watched changed what you did, even though nobody said anything. You will supply the panopticon before you read it.

## Paired with Fanon

Foucault describes a general condition; [[entities/frantz-fanon|Fanon]] describes a distributed one. Not everyone is seen the same way, and a theory of visibility that cannot register that difference is one this course sets out to question. Fanon is not simply an illustration of Foucault.

## Set text

The panopticon extract from *Discipline and Punish* — see [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]] · [[entities/frantz-fanon]] · [[concepts/naturalization]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7]]

entities/plato.md.body:
# Plato

**c. 428 to 348 BCE.**

## The claim in one line

What we take for reality may be appearances, and there may be a level of reality that appearances imperfectly reflect.

## Quote

> They would believe that the shadows of the objects were the truth.

## How the course uses him

The cave is used to force [[concepts/the-ontological-turn|the ontological turn]]. The productive question is not whether Plato is right but **whether our situation is the same as the prisoners' or different, and what would count as evidence either way.**

Three questions carry the session:

- Is our situation the same as theirs, or different?
- You have never seen a perfect circle, only approximately circular things — where does the knowledge of a perfect circle come from?
- **Is the prisoner who leaves better off than the ones who stay?** ("The prisoner who leaves is worse off, because he cannot go back" — this is Plato's own worry, and worth taking seriously.)

## Where he returns

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] and [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] both use the W04 question as the structural template: **is the difference essential, or is it just where we currently stand?** The same argument runs through these topics.

## Set text

The Allegory of the Cave, *Republic* VII, in a clean modern translation, roughly two pages. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[concepts/the-ontological-turn]] · [[concepts/the-gap]]

entities/john-berger.md.body:
# John Berger

**1926 to 2017.**

## The claim in one line

The way we see things is affected by what you know or believe, so **seeing is never a neutral reception of what is there.**

## Quote

> We never look at just one thing; we are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves.

## In this course

Berger opens the course. His sentence appears in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]].

A question to consider: *Berger says we never look at one thing, we look at the relation between things and ourselves. Is that true of a photograph of a stranger?*

## Set text

*Ways of Seeing*, chapter 1, first six pages. If you find the prose difficult, the BBC episode of the same name is offered as a second entry point in the first session. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Also taught in Art Appreciation

Berger anchors [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-10-berger-and-the-reproduction|Art Appreciation L10]] ("a reproduction is not a neutral copy"). The two courses take different chapters of the same argument: Art Appreciation runs Berger on **reproduction**, Oxbridge runs him on **perception**.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]] · [[concepts/framework]]

entities/sigmund-freud.md.body:
# Sigmund Freud

**1856 to 1939.**

## The claim in one line

Forgetting is **active work rather than decay**; what is pushed down returns in distorted forms, and part of what shapes you is inaccessible to you.

## Quote

> The repressed does not disappear; it returns.

## How the course uses him

Freud is **paired with [[entities/henri-bergson]] in week 10**, so that two incompatible accounts arrive at the same conclusion: **forgetting is a function of memory, not a failure of it.**

The question his account produces is one you may find hard to answer comfortably:

> If forgetting is something you **do** rather than something that happens to you, **are you responsible for what you forget?**

In **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|week 9]]** he supplies the second objection to machine minds: **a system whose weights can be inspected has no unconscious** in this sense. Like Bergson's duration objection, this is tested for whether it names a difference in kind or in current engineering.

## Reading

Freud on repression and the return of the repressed is on the extension list. It is not assigned.

## Note on scope

The course uses one Freudian claim and does not teach psychoanalysis. Nothing here asks you to accept the wider theory. The session is not about memory techniques, and it is not about therapy.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[entities/henri-bergson]]

entities/tobias-rees.md.body:
# Tobias Rees

**Contemporary.**

## The claim in one line

AI breaks concepts that defined the modern period, because **agency, creativity, knowledge, language, and understanding turn out to be separable from being alive or being human.**

## Key quote

> AI can have agency, creativity, knowledge, language and understanding without either being alive or being human.

Two further lines:

> AI defies many of the most fundamental, most taken-for-granted concepts that have defined the modern period.

> Deep learning systems have qualities that, up until recently, were considered possible only for living organisms in general and for humans in particular.

## How this course uses him

Rees is the set text for week 9.

The question his lines are aimed at: *if agency and understanding can come apart from being alive, were they ever properties of life — or properties we assigned to life because we had no other examples?*

## The counterweight

The session does not leave Rees unopposed. [[entities/henri-bergson]] supplies duration (a system that can be reset has no duration) and [[entities/sigmund-freud]] supplies the unconscious (a system whose weights can be inspected has none). Both objections are then put under the same test: **are these differences in kind, or in current engineering?**

## The Snell move

Rees points toward the claim that the interior self was not available to Homeric Greeks and was constituted over centuries partly by writing. If something that fundamental can be produced by a technology, **what might AI be producing right now that we cannot yet see?**

## Preparation

Three guiding questions come with the text:

1. What concept does Rees think AI breaks?
2. Is his claim about machines or about us?
3. Where does his argument go too far?

## Set text

The Noema essay on AI and the concepts of the modern period — see [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[entities/benjamin-bratton]] · [[entities/donna-haraway]]

# Oxbridge W05: Is the Gap a Loss, a Liberation, or a Condition?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2: The Gap]] · Week 5 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|← W04]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Given that no representation reaches the thing itself, how should we live? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | **None.** Four quotations, delivered live |
| Prepared | Arrive with a position and a case, from W04's closing question |
| Carried out | Things considered real in the past are now considered false. Were we wrong then, or did reality change? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Take one of the three readings of the gap and defend it against the other two
2. Work from four quotations delivered live, without a text to prepare against
3. Move from an epistemological claim to a claim about how to live, and notice they are different moves

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

The question is already on the board from last session. Write your position and one reason. Two minutes, silent.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

You give your position in one sentence. The room is sorted into three columns on the board: loss · liberation · condition.

| Column | The claim | Push |
|---|---|---|
| **Loss** | "There is a real world and we are locked out of it" | Locked out implies you know what is on the other side. **How?** |
| **Liberation** | "If there is no fixed reality, we get to make one" | Make one **out of what**? |
| **Condition** | "It is just what having a mind is like" | If it is simply the condition, why does it feel like a loss to so many people? |

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

Four quotations, introduced one at a time. Each names a position you may already occupy.

### [[entities/jean-paul-sartre|Sartre]]

> Man is condemned to be free.

If there is no essence, no given nature, no original to return to, is the gap even a loss? Can you lose something that never existed? Sartre calls it a condemnation, not a gift. Why the harsh word, if freedom is good?

### [[entities/albert-camus|Camus]]

> The absurd is born of the confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.

Camus locates the absurd **in the meeting** — not in us and not in the world. Does that change anything? Is revolt a position you could actually hold, or only a mood?

### Heidegger

We are always already thrown into a world we did not choose, with tools and frameworks that were there before us.

If the framework is what makes understanding **possible** rather than what blocks it, does the word "gap" still fit? **Is a lens an obstacle to sight?**

### Camus again

> We must imagine Sisyphus happy.

Is that convincing, or is it a rhetorical trick? Is happiness inside the condition the same as accepting a loss?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

Return to your column. Anyone who wants to move must say which quotation moved them and why.

> [!note] Changing your mind is the point
> Moving under argument is the skill being trained here. In this session, changing your mind is an achievement, not a lapse. It rehearses the second interview move (*absorb the push without abandoning the claim*) and **movement**, the fourth quality the course names.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> Things considered real in the past are now considered false. Were we wrong then, or did reality change?

## Links

[[entities/jean-paul-sartre]] · [[entities/albert-camus]] · [[concepts/the-gap]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]]

# Oxbridge W10: What Survives Forgetting?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5: Memory and Forgetting]] · Week 10 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|← W09]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is forgetting a failure of memory, or a function of it? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | none |
| Prepare | Bring **one memory from before you were ten**, and be willing to describe it out loud |
| Carried out | Money is real. Borders are real. Weekends are real. Who agreed? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Argue whether forgetting is a failure of memory or a function of it
2. Use your own memory as evidence without turning the session into anecdote
3. Say what survives when the record does not

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> Describe a memory from before you were ten. Then write down **how you know it happened**.

Two minutes, silent.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

- How many of you are describing the event, and how many are describing **a photograph, a story you were told, or a previous time you remembered it**?
- Has anyone here discovered that a memory they trusted was wrong?
- Does clarity track accuracy anywhere else? Are your clearest dreams your truest ones?

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

### The painted sheet

> Remembering is not retrieval from storage. It is repainting a surface, and the new paint covers the old. After twenty years of remembering, what you have is the last painting, made from the previous painting, **not the event**.

- If that is true, is a memory you have revisited often more reliable **or less**?
- Is a memory you have never revisited preserved, or simply gone?
- What is the difference between remembering something and **remembering remembering it**?

### [[entities/henri-bergson|Bergson]]

Habit memory is performed by the body: you do not recall how to ride a bicycle, you do it. Pure memory survives whole, and attention filters it rather than losing it. On this account we forget nothing; we simply cannot attend to most of it.

If nothing is lost and only access fails, does that make forgetting **less serious or more**?

### [[entities/sigmund-freud|Freud]]

Forgetting is work. Things are pushed down, and they return in distorted forms: slips, dreams, repetitions.

If forgetting is something you **do** rather than something that happens to you, are you responsible for what you forget?

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

Is forgetting a failure of memory or a function of it? One sentence.

Then the harder version, connecting back to W09:

> If a machine forgot the way a body forgets, by accumulating distortion rather than deleting files, would the human and machine line still hold?

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> Money is real. Borders are real. Weekends are real. Who agreed?

## Links

[[entities/henri-bergson]] · [[entities/sigmund-freud]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11]]

# Oxbridge W09: Is the Human and Machine Line Essential or Contingent?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4: The Body and the Machine]] · Week 9 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|← W08]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | When you say a machine cannot do something, are you describing what a mind necessarily is, or what technology currently happens to be? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/tobias-rees\|Rees]], Noema — with three guiding questions sent in advance |
| Carried through | Human memory is repainted every time it is used. Machine memory is a record that can be loaded or deleted. Is that a difference in kind? |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you can:

1. Tell the difference between describing what a mind necessarily is and describing what technology currently happens to be
2. Use Rees to locate where the line has already moved
3. Argue whether repainted human memory and loadable machine memory differ in kind or in degree

## Before class

Read Rees in Noema, and prepare answers to three questions:

1. What concept does Rees think AI breaks?
2. Is his claim about machines or about us?
3. **Where does his argument go too far?**

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> Write down one thing you can do that a machine cannot.

Two minutes, silent. Answers are collected on the board.

## Movement 1 · elicit (10 minutes)

Work down the list. For each item, two questions:

- **What exactly would a machine have to do for you to withdraw this item?**
- Has any item on this list been withdrawn in the last ten years?

| If you say | Consider |
|---|---|
| "Feel" | What would count as evidence of feeling **in anything, including another person**? |
| "Understand rather than predict" | Describe a test that separates them. If you cannot, is the distinction doing work? |
| "Have a body" | This connects to W08. Robots have bodies — is the objection about bodies or about **being alive**? |
| "Create something new" | What would count as new? Is any human creation not a recombination? |

## Movement 2 · complicate (15 minutes)

### Rees

Three lines:

> AI defies many of the most fundamental, most taken-for-granted concepts that have defined the modern period.

> Deep learning systems have qualities that, up until recently, were considered possible only for living organisms in general and for humans in particular.

> AI can have agency, creativity, knowledge, language and understanding without either being alive or being human.

**Question.** If agency and understanding can come apart from being alive, **were they ever properties of life, or properties we assigned to life because we had no other examples?**

### Bergson and Freud as counterweight

- **[[entities/henri-bergson]]:** lived time is duration, accumulated and indivisible, not a sequence of states. **A system that can be reset to a previous state has no duration.**
- **[[entities/sigmund-freud]]:** there is a part of you that you did not author and cannot access, which shapes what you do. **A system whose weights can be inspected has no unconscious in that sense.**

**Questions.** Are these differences in kind or in current engineering? **If a system accumulated distortion instead of storing records, would either objection survive?** (That question is [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]] in advance.)

### The Snell move

Rees points toward the claim that the interior self, the sense of having an inner life, was not available to Homeric Greeks and was constituted over centuries partly by writing.

**Question.** If something that fundamental can be produced by a technology, **what might AI be producing right now that we cannot yet see?**

## Movement 3 · commit (10 minutes)

**Question.** Is the human and machine distinction essential or contingent? One sentence.

Both sides get pushed:

- If you argue it is essential, you must **name the property**.
- If you argue it is contingent, you must say whether *any* distinction could ever be essential on your view, or whether you have made the word meaningless.

## Closing question (5 minutes)

> Human memory is repainted every time it is used. Machine memory is a record that can be loaded or deleted. Is that a difference in kind?

## Links

[[entities/tobias-rees]] · [[entities/henri-bergson]] · [[entities/sigmund-freud]] · [[concepts/situated-knowledge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]]

# Oxbridge W14: Is a View from Nowhere Possible?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8: Synthesis]] · Week 14 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|← W13]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | The title echoes Nagel and names the course throughline in five words |
| Duration | 45 minutes: four questions at about 10 minutes each |
| Reading | None. Think back over the term — your notes and the group-chat thread |
| Prepare | A position you have changed your mind about |
| In session | You answer a question instead of carrying one out |

## Objectives

By the end of this lesson you can:

1. Name a position you have changed your mind about over the term, and say what changed it
2. Answer a question directly, rather than carrying it out
3. Say what the throughline of the course was, in your own words

## Opening prompt (5 minutes)

> What does the world look like?

Two minutes, silent. A plain question that will produce fourteen weeks of material in one line each.

## The four questions

One question at a time, roughly ten minutes each.

### 1. Is an unframed view of anything even possible?

Every framework this term hid the edges that made it a framework rather than reality: the map, [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]], the body, machine cognition, the categories that decide who counts.

If science is also a chosen set of exclusions, what distinguishes a good frame from a bad one, if not closeness to an unframed reality nobody can access? This is the W04 question returning, and [[concepts/situated-knowledge|situated knowledge]] is a third option between neutral science and total relativism.

### 2. Does the human and machine line survive its own test?

We drew the line at memory: human memory is sedimented and repainted, machine memory is a clean record. If a system learned the way a body learns, through accumulation and distortion rather than storage, would the distinction hold — or were we only describing what AI happens to be right now? This is structurally identical to the Plato question from Week 4.

### 3. Whose agreement made this real?

Take any object in the room and trace it back to power, not just agreement. Then ask whether power and agreement are different things or the same thing described from two positions.

### 4. Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework?

The hardest move, and the reason this session exists. Apply the course's suspicion to the course itself.

- If every position is framed, is that claim framed? If it is, why should we accept it? If it is not, you have found your view from nowhere.
- Has this course given you a better view, or only a different one? What would tell you which?
- Is the suspicion useful, or does it end in a place where nothing can be said?

## Closing (5 minutes)

For the first time in fourteen weeks, you answer a question instead of carrying one out.

> Say one thing you now believe that you did not believe at the start of the course, and say what changed it.

## Links

[[concepts/view-from-nowhere]] · [[concepts/situated-knowledge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8]] · [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|Question Bank]] · [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]]

# Oxbridge Unit 4: The Body and the Machine

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 4 of 8 · Weeks 8–9 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|← Unit 3]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5 →]]

## Unit question

**Where does the thinking thing end?**

## How the two sessions connect

Both sessions ask the same question: **is a boundary essential or contingent?** Week 8 asks whether the body is a reliable instrument or a framework like any other. Week 9 asks whether the line between human and machine is a real difference in kind, or just a description of where technology currently stands.

The link between them:

> What a body can do and what a machine can do turn out to be the same kind of question. Both are about mapping capacities, not testing essences.

## Week 8: the body

[[entities/maurice-merleau-ponty]] gives the anchor: the body is our general medium for having a world. If that is true, what happens when the medium is wrong?

You work through four cases, one at a time: **phantom limb, chronic pain without injury, synaesthesia, thermal adaptation.** Each breaks a different escape route. The session closes on Spinoza's reframe — stop asking what a body **is** and ask what a body **can do**.

## Week 9: the machine

[[entities/tobias-rees]] argues that AI defies concepts that have defined the modern period; that deep learning systems have qualities previously thought possible only for living things; and that a system can have agency, creativity, knowledge, language and understanding without being alive or human.

[[entities/henri-bergson]] and [[entities/sigmund-freud]] supply the counterweight — **duration** and **the unconscious** as things a system without a history cannot have. [[entities/donna-haraway]] and [[entities/benjamin-bratton]] extend the argument outward.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08: Can the body be trusted?]] — describe being cold without the word cold and without a number. Four cases, then Spinoza.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09: Is the human and machine line essential or contingent?]] — the whole session is one list, written by you in the first two minutes.

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated Knowledge]]

## Preparation

For W08 you receive one quotation in advance. For W09 you receive the Rees essay with three guiding questions; the third ("where does his argument go too far?") invites disagreement before you open the text.

Nothing is written or collected: the course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]].

## Bridge to Unit 5

W09 closes on a carried question: human memory is sedimented and repainted while machine memory is a clean record. That question is taken up in [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5]].

# Oxbridge Unit 5: Memory and Forgetting

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 5 of 8 · Week 10 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|← Unit 4]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6 →]]

## Unit question

**What survives forgetting?**

This is a one-session unit. It tests one claim: that human memory is repainted while machine memory is a clean record.

## The image to work from

> A painted sheet. Each time you remember something, you do not retrieve a stored file. You repaint the surface, and the new paint covers the old. What you have after twenty years of remembering is not the event. It is the last painting, made from the previous painting.

## The two philosophers

Two incompatible accounts that arrive at the same conclusion from opposite directions:

- **[[entities/henri-bergson]]** separates *habit memory*, which the body performs, from *pure memory*, which survives whole and is filtered out by attention rather than lost. On this account we forget nothing; we simply cannot attend to most of it.
- **[[entities/sigmund-freud]]** proposes that forgetting is not decay but active work: things are pushed down, and they return in distorted form.

> [!note] The shared conclusion
> The same conclusion arrives from two directions. **Forgetting is not the failure of memory. It is a function of it.**

The two accounts are incompatible and converge anyway. This is the course's cleanest example of an argument that does not depend on picking a winner.

## Session

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10: What survives forgetting?]] — you bring a memory from before you were ten, and discover how many people are describing a photograph or a story.

## Concepts introduced

None new. The unit works with concepts already introduced — [[concepts/the-gap|the gap]] applied to your own past, and [[concepts/framework|framework]] applied to attention.

## Preparation

No reading. Bring **one memory from before you were ten**, and be willing to describe it out loud. This is the only session whose preparation is personal rather than textual.

Nothing is written or collected: the course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]].

## In this session

- The session is personal, which is a resource. You describe rather than argue, then convert that into argument later in the session.
- This is not a discussion of memory techniques or exam revision. The question is not how to remember better; it is what memory is for.
- The session builds on Week 9: if a machine forgot the way a body forgets — by accumulating distortion rather than deleting files — would the human/machine line still hold?

## Bridge to Unit 6

> If each person's past is repainted privately, the question becomes how any two people share anything at all.

W10 closes on the question that opens the next unit: *money is real, borders are real, weekends are real — who agreed?* [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6]].
