# Art Appreciation S1 End of Term: The Retrospective

[[classes/art-appreciation/art-appreciation|Art Appreciation]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/assessments/art-appreciation-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-14-the-retrospective|Lesson 14]] · End of Term Exam category, 20%

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Tue 2027-01-05, the Tuesday double, **in class** |
| Category | End of Term Exam, 20% of the semester grade |
| Format | In-class constellation: the whole semester laid out as one argument |
| The task | Show a semester of looking as one argument, **with the argument in the layout** |
| Marked on | Selection · Adjacency reasoning · Legibility of the argument in the layout · The written argument · Defending your choices |
| Brought with you | Three works that changed how you see, with reasons (the break homework) |
| Criteria issued | Before the break, with the homework |
| Available to you | Everything you have made. The Unit 1 boards and Unit 4 syntheses go back on the walls before Monday |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Lay the semester out and see it **as one body of work rather than four units**.
2. **Defend your three works to someone who chose differently**, and not simply concede.
3. Show a semester of looking as one argument, with the argument in the layout.

## The task

The whole semester, read back as one argument.

This is the **third constellation of the year**, and it is the one where the method should finally look like a method rather than a rule you were following.

Over the break you chose **three works that changed how you see**, with reasons. That choice is the seed. In the session you build a constellation that makes an argument about the semester itself: what you now see that you did not see in September, and what the sequence of the year did to your looking.

Everything you have made is available. The Unit 1 boards and the Unit 4 syntheses are back on the walls before Monday, so your earlier work is in the room with you.

## Instructions

1. **Bring your three works and your reasons.** This is the break homework and it is the entry ticket, worth 3 to 4 hours across the holiday.
2. **Build the constellation.** Adjacency is still the argument, as it has been since A1.
3. **Use your own earlier work.** The boards and syntheses on the walls are material, not decoration.
4. **Be ready to defend.** Somebody in the room chose differently, and you will be asked to hold your ground rather than politely agree. Conceding immediately is not generosity, it is a failure to argue.
5. **Write the argument** the layout makes.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). This is a 20% category and there is no second sitting.

## Rubric

Five criteria, equally weighted. The first four are the constellation skills the course has built since September; the fifth is new and only possible at the end.

| | **Selection** | **Adjacency reasoning** | **Layout legibility** | **The written argument** | **Defending your choices** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | Three works chosen because of what they changed, not because they were liked. The reasons are specific to the change | Every pairing carries a reason belonging to that pair alone. The semester's tensions are held rather than smoothed | The argument about the semester is visible on arrival. The layout is doing work the writing does not have to repeat | Argues what the semester did to your looking, and names what is still unresolved | Holds a position under real disagreement, gives ground only for a reason, and can say what would change their mind |
| **Convincing** | Three well-chosen works with clear reasons | Reasons specific to their pairs, one or two transferable | The argument reads clearly with a moment's looking | A clear argument about the semester, supported | Defends the choices with reasons, with some retreat under pressure |
| **Competent** | Three works chosen on preference, with reasons attached afterwards | Related pairings with true but general reasons | An order is visible; the argument needs help | States what changed, supports part of it | Explains the choices, concedes quickly |
| **Partial** | Three works, reasons thin | Grouped by theme | Reads as a collection of the year's work | Narrates the semester | Cannot say why these three rather than three others |
| **Undeveloped** | Selection incomplete or arbitrary | No reasoning | No argument discernible | Little writing | No defense offered |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade rather than a raw score.

## Why it is in class and not in the exam window

The school exam window is Mon 2027-01-11 to Mon 2027-01-18. This retrospective sits **Tue 2027-01-05**, in class, before it.

The assessment is a constellation build: it needs the room, the walls, the pinned earlier work and the students arguing with each other. None of that survives being moved into an exam hall.

## After the sit

- The protocol, as always: **criteria**, **ten minutes of silence**, **one named strength**, **one move.**

- Semester 2 opens on the art-world arc and the Atlas Book capstone. The retrospective is where its first material comes from.

# 9607 S1 A2: Blog Mid-Point

[[classes/media-studies/media-studies|Media Studies]] · [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-08-representation-applied-to-your-own-product|Lesson 08]] · Attainment 2 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Due | Mon 2026-10-26, in the first five minutes of class |
| Category | Attainment, the second of four in the 50% category |
| Format | Submitted work, not a sitting. You hand in a URL |
| Assesses | **AO3**, the research and planning strand of Component 1 |
| What is submitted | Your production blog, posts 1 to 7, complete and to standard |
| Feeds | A3, the complete Component 1 portfolio, and the mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29 |
| Unit | [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-4-representation\|U4 Representation]] (it lands in U4's first session; the work belongs to the C1 production) |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Keep a production blog as a **dated record made on the day**, not a reconstruction written the night before a deadline.
2. Research real professional products and show what you took from them.
3. Profile a real audience for your product with evidence, rather than describing "everyone".
4. Plan a production in enough detail that someone else could shoot it.
5. Label your own contribution honestly where the work is group work.

## The task

Your Component 1 blog is the process evidence for the whole coursework component. A2 is its mid-point check: posts 1 to 7, complete, to standard, on the day.

The seven posts:

| # | Post |
|---|---|
| 1 | Brief and group registered |
| 2 | Research into similar professional products |
| 3 | Audience profile |
| 4 | Pitch |
| 5 | Planning suite |
| 6 | Production log opened |
| 7 | Early production evidence |

Three rules apply to all seven: **every post dated on the day it happened**, **individual contributions labeled**, and **no gaps**.

Submission is undramatic. You post the URL in the first five minutes of class on Monday. There is no ceremony and no presentation.

## Instructions

1. Finish posts 1 to 7 to standard over the week before the deadline. Homework from Lesson 07 is exactly this.
2. Use the **mid-point checklist** to check yourself. It is the same instrument A2 is marked with, so there is no mystery about the standard.
3. **CS5, the peer blog audit on Wed 2026-10-21**, runs against that same checklist. Whatever your peer finds is what your teacher will find. Fix it before Monday.
4. Check every URL from a signed-out browser. A blog nobody but you can open is not submitted.
5. Post the URL on Mon 10-26 in the first five minutes.

**Backdating is not allowed and is visible.** Posts are dated the day the work happened. A blog that appears all at once the night before evidences AO3 at the bottom of the range no matter how good the content is, because the point of process evidence is that it records a process.

**If you are absent.** Contact your teacher **at least 24 hours before** the deadline; extensions are also requested 24 hours ahead. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). A blog is submitted by URL, so absence is rarely a reason for lateness.

## Rubric

A2 samples the **research and planning column** of Cambridge's Component 1 criteria: *Research, plan and apply knowledge and understanding*, one of the five 10-mark strands of the 50-mark component (AO3).

Cambridge's own bands for that strand, from the 2027 syllabus:

| Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|
| **9–10** | **Sophisticated** research into appropriate professional products · varied and detailed planning **fully** meeting the requirements of the brief · sophisticated implementation of research showing insightful understanding of the key concepts |
| **7–8** | **Thorough** research into appropriate professional products · effective planning appropriate to the requirements of the brief · thorough implementation of research showing effective understanding of the key concepts |
| **5–6** | **Clear** research into appropriate professional products · appropriate planning meeting the requirements of the brief · implementation of research showing clear understanding of the key concepts |
| **3–4** | **Limited** research · generally appropriate planning meeting **some** of the requirements of the brief · implementation showing limited understanding of the key concepts |
| **1–2** | **Basic** research · limited planning meeting **few** of the requirements of the brief · implementation showing minimal understanding of the key concepts |
| **0** | No creditable content |

The phrase that decides most marks is **"implementation of research"**. Research that sits in post 2 and never reappears is research nobody implemented. The top bands need your planning and your early production evidence to visibly carry what the research taught you. A blog can be thorough and still land at 5 or 6 if posts 2 and 5 do not talk to each other.

At the mid-point the checklist's three mechanical rules are also gatekeepers: undated posts, unlabeled contributions and gaps all read as incomplete process evidence.

Your mark is curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw.

## After the sit

- Marking starts the same night, because **mid-term grades are due Thu 2026-10-29**. A2 is the attainment that feeds them.
- Whatever A2 finds is the thing to fix before A3 on Fri 2026-11-27, when the same blog is marked again as part of the complete portfolio. Nothing about A2 is final: it is a mid-point precisely so the second half can be better.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS5**, the peer blog audit (Wed 2026-10-21) | The dress rehearsal, run on the real instrument, with working days to spare |
| The **mid-point checklist** from Lesson 07 | Self-check, post by post |
| **HW1**, the break production window | Posts 6 and 7 exist because of it |
| Lesson 07's reading-order and PEEM work | Post 2's research needs to read texts, not list them |
| [[concepts/process-evidence-and-reflection\|Process evidence and reflection]] | Why the blog is assessed at all, and what it is evidence of |

# 9607 S1 A1: Timed Media Language Analysis

[[classes/media-studies/media-studies|Media Studies]] · [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-06-a1-timed-media-language-analysis|Lesson 06]] · Attainment 1 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Wed 2026-10-14, the Wednesday double |
| Category | Attainment, the first of four in the 50% category |
| Format | Written analysis of an unseen TV-drama extract, under exam conditions |
| Length | 60 minutes of writing |
| Marks | 25, on the official Cambridge Paper 2 Section A criteria |
| Assesses | AO1 and AO2 |
| Extract | 2 to 3 minutes, screened four times in the room. You have not seen it before and it is not a text taught to this class |
| You may bring | Your own code checklist. Nothing else |
| Feeds | AS Component 2 Section A, and the mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29 |
| Returned | Within five working days |
| Unit | [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-3-macro-and-textual-analysis\|U3 Macro and Textual Analysis]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show, in writing and without help, that you can:

1. Analyze an extract you have never seen, naming how camera, sound, mise-en-scène and editing construct its meaning.
2. Tie every observation to an effect. A technique that is named but not explained does not count.
3. Cover all four code families systematically rather than writing at length about the one you noticed first.
4. Use precise media terminology throughout, including the sound and editing vocabulary, not only the camera terms.
5. Where you bring in a theory or a context, say where the extract complicates it as well as where it fits.
6. Sustain 60 minutes of continuous analytical writing under exam conditions.

## The task

You are given an unseen extract from a television drama, 2 to 3 minutes long, and the Paper 2 Section A prompt: analyze how the extract constructs meaning through camera, sound, mise-en-scène and editing. It is the same wording as the real examination.

The extract is deliberately unfamiliar. Everything you need in order to read it has been taught since Week 1: signs and codes ([[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-03-sign-types-and-codes|L03]]), genre and camera ([[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-04-genre-and-camera|L04]]), narrative under load ([[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-05-narrative-and-the-planning-lock|L05]]), and the four-pass [[concepts/the-viewing-protocol|viewing protocol]]. What is new is the text, not the skill.

## Instructions

**Before the sit.** Bring your personal code checklist, the one you built from the L03 exit ticket. It is collected at the door and handed back to you at your desk, because systematic coverage is one of the things this assessment samples. Review your strain log from the two lessons before this one.

**In the room.**

1. Conditions are briefed once, then the room goes silent.
2. The extract is screened **four times**, following the examination's own protocol: watch the first time without writing, then take a note pass on each of the three remaining screenings.
3. Write for **60 minutes**, continuously.
4. Hand in your script. Unfinished at 60 minutes is submitted at 60 minutes. The timebox is part of what this samples.

**Writing the answer.** Work through the code families, not through the extract's timeline. For each observation, name the technique, point to the exact moment, and say what it does to the viewer. One well-chosen moment analyzed properly is worth more than five moments listed. If you use Propp or Todorov, include at least one sentence on where the extract strains the model.

**If you are absent or need an extension.** Contact your teacher **at least 24 hours before** the sitting. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact, the mark may be 0, and that rule applies even when the absence is genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). Extensions are also requested 24 hours ahead. See [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework]].

## Rubric

Marked on the **official Cambridge Paper 2 criteria**. Five criteria, 25 marks, and each criterion is banded **independently** on a best-fit basis. A script can sit in different bands on different criteria, so a strong terminology mark does not lift a weak analysis mark.

| # | Criterion | AO | Marks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Media Concepts (language and representation) | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 2 | Contexts and Critical Debates (social significances) | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 3 | Use of Terminology | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 4 | Analysis of how meaning is created, including use of theory | AO2 | 0 to 5 |
| 5 | Use of Examples | AO2 | 0 to 5 |

Totals: **AO1 15, AO2 10.** Cambridge's band words, per criterion: **5** sophisticated or insightful · **4** thorough or effective · **3** clear or appropriate · **2** limited · **1** basic · **0** no creditable content.

### What each band looks like in this task

The five criteria and their band words are Cambridge's. The descriptions in this table are written for this course so that the criteria are checkable before you write, not only after you are marked. They show how the bands are applied here; they are not Cambridge's published wording.

| Criterion | Band 5 | Band 3 | Band 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Media Concepts** | Reads language and representation together: the technical choices are shown doing something to who or what is represented | Applies media language accurately, but representation is handled separately from the technical reading, or briefly | Concepts are named without being applied to this extract |
| **Contexts and Critical Debates** | Genre, industry or audience context is used to explain a specific choice, and any theory used is tested against the extract, including where it strains | One relevant context is stated and connected to at least one choice | Context is asserted and left unconnected |
| **Use of Terminology** | Precise throughout, sound and editing included, used because it is the shortest accurate description available | Correct in the familiar areas, camera and mise-en-scène, thinner on sound and editing | Everyday description with occasional labels attached |
| **Analysis of meaning** | Every observation reaches an effect. Nothing is listed | Most observations reach an effect, some stop at description | What happens is described, and the meaning is left implied |
| **Use of Examples** | Specific moments, described precisely enough that a marker can find them, drawn from all four code families | Real examples, unevenly distributed across the code families | Examples are general or refer to the extract as a whole |

### How the mark becomes a grade

The 25-mark total is **not** what is recorded as your grade. Attainments are curved against CIE past-paper data, allowing for where the class is in its learning, so the grade reflects your trajectory rather than what the script would score on a Cambridge paper today. You will always be told how the boundaries and curve were set. The grade scale is on [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework]].

Two things worth knowing now: this is one of **four** attainments this semester, and because the course runs four rather than six, **no lowest attainment can be dropped.** That is a fact about how the course is built, not about conduct.

## After the sit

- Scripts come back within **five working days**.
- You self-assess against the mark scheme **before** any discussion of marks. This is not optional: the target is that your own banding lands within one band of the teacher's.
- You then log **exactly one** target, in your own words. It is retrieved and checked at the next assessment.
- The full review runs at [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-07-reading-systematically-toward-the-blog-midpoint|L07]]. A1 also feeds the mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS4**, the genre and camera paragraph (Wed 2026-09-23) | The direct rehearsal for this task. Reread the feedback on it before the sit |
| Your **code checklist** from L03 | Systematic coverage. Bring it |
| The **strain log** from the two lessons before the sit | Your theory sentences, ready made |
| The **four-pass viewing protocol** | How to use the three note-taking screenings |
| Coursebook §4.1 to §4.3 | The anatomy of this exact task: the prompt, the screening protocol, micro against macro, and essay architecture |
| Pairing-sentence practice | Fusing content and technique into one sentence, which is what band 4 and 5 analysis reads like |

# 9607 S1 A3: Component 1 Portfolio

[[classes/media-studies/media-studies|Media Studies]] · [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-11-audiences-and-the-portfolio-submission|Lesson 11]] · Attainment 3 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Due | Fri 2026-11-27, submitted in session. **No edits after** |
| Category | Attainment, the third of four in the 50% category. The largest piece of work in the semester |
| Format | The complete Component 1 Foundation Portfolio: product, Creative Critical Reflection, dated blog |
| Assesses | **AO3 (40 marks) + AO2 (10 marks)**, the full 50-mark component |
| Returned | Tue 2026-12-01, self-assessment first |
| Feeds | Your Component 1 grade, and the production targets Semester 2 collects on |
| Unit | [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-5-media-contexts\|U5 Media Contexts]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Finish a media product that works for a real audience, in a real genre, to a standard an audience would accept.
2. Use technical skills well enough that the craft does not distract from the meaning.
3. Show research and planning that visibly shaped what you made.
4. Produce a Creative Critical Reflection that is itself a media product, not an essay in disguise.
5. Analyze your own work honestly, with evidence, including where it did not succeed.
6. Submit complete and on time, with every post dated and every contribution labeled.

## The task

A3 is the whole of Component 1. You submit three things together:

**1. The product.** Your finished film opening or magazine, exported and playable, in the genre you registered.

**2. The Creative Critical Reflection (CCR).** Your reflection **in a creative format**, posted. It answers the four set questions and is assessed on its own technical and creative skill as well as on what it says. A CCR read off a page as a talking head is answering the questions while failing the format.

**3. The blog, complete.** Every post, dated on the day, contributions labeled, no gaps. This is the same blog A2 sampled at its mid-point, now finished.

## Instructions

**The week is built around Friday.**

1. **Wed 11-25, the double: CCR surgery.** The last window where help is available. The queue runs in **triage order by CS7 severity**, not by hand-raising, so everyone is seen and the strongest drafts get peer support rather than teacher time. Every visit ends with **one fix executed**, not promised.
2. **The submission checklist**, run at the close of Wednesday: product exported and playable · CCR in its creative format, posted · blog complete, posts dated, contributions labeled · URLs correct.
3. **Fri 11-27: submission.** Final checks against the checklist, URLs and files logged on the submission sheet, confirmation shown on screen per group.
4. **No edits after.** This is absolute. Friday is logistics, not heroics.

**If you are absent.** Contact your teacher **at least 24 hours before** the deadline; extensions are requested 24 hours ahead. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

**Group work.** Where the production is group work, individual contributions must be labeled in the blog. The CCR is your own.

## Rubric

Cambridge's **Component 1 assessment criteria**, 2027 syllabus. Five strands of 10 marks, **50 marks total**: four strands are AO3 Practical Application (40 marks), one is AO2 Evaluation (10 marks).

| Strand | AO | What it judges | Marks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | AO3 | **Use appropriate media language** to communicate meaning to an intended audience | 10 |
| 2 | AO3 | **Use technical skills effectively** to express and communicate ideas | 10 |
| 3 | AO3 | **Research, plan and apply** knowledge and understanding | 10 |
| 4 | AO3 | **Creative Critical Reflection skills**: technical and creative skill in the CCR itself | 10 |
| 5 | AO2 | **Analyse and evaluate own work**, supported with relevant textual evidence | 10 |

Every strand runs on the same band ladder: **9–10 sophisticated · 7–8 effective or thorough · 5–6 clear · 3–4 limited or general · 1–2 basic or minimal · 0 no creditable content.** Strands are banded separately, so a strong product does not carry a weak CCR.

### The bands, strand by strand

| Marks | Media language (1) | Technical skills (2) | Research and planning (3) | CCR skills (4) | Evaluation (5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **9–10** | Sophisticated use of media language, insightful engagement with audience; targets the intended audience with sophistication and is **entirely convincing** as a film opening or magazine | Production is sophisticated, highly appropriate, and accurately follows or **knowingly subverts** genre codes; technical elements sophisticatedly handled, finished to a high standard | Sophisticated research into professional products; varied and detailed planning **fully** meeting the brief; sophisticated implementation showing insightful understanding of the key concepts | Sophisticated technical skills throughout, with a **wide range** of creative approaches, sophisticatedly engaging the audience | Sophisticated understanding of how meaning is created; insightful critical comment on own successes, fully supported with a wide range of examples; sophisticated engagement with **all four** questions |
| **7–8** | Effective use of media language, appropriate engagement; targets audience effectively and is effective in convincing | Production is effective and effectively follows or subverts genre codes; technical elements effectively handled, **mostly** finished to a high standard | Thorough research; effective planning appropriate to the brief; thorough implementation showing effective understanding | Effective technical skills throughout, with **a range** of creative approaches, effectively engaging the audience | Thorough understanding; appropriate critical comment, effectively supported with a range of examples; thorough engagement with all four questions |
| **5–6** | Clear use of media language, **some** engagement; targets audience appropriately and is **mostly** convincing | Production is appropriate and mostly follows or subverts genre codes; technical elements effectively handled, **sometimes** finished to a high standard | Clear research; appropriate planning meeting the brief; implementation showing clear understanding | Clear technical skills, with **more than one** creative approach, mostly engaging the audience | Clear understanding; appropriate critical comment, appropriately supported with examples; clear engagement with all four questions |
| **3–4** | Limited use of media language, **general** engagement; simply targets audience, generally appropriate as a film opening or magazine | Production is limited, generally follows or subverts codes **with limited success**; technical elements generally handled, production is complete | Limited research; generally appropriate planning meeting **some** requirements; implementation showing limited understanding | Limited technical skills, **often only one** creative approach, sometimes engaging the audience | Limited understanding; generally supported with limited examples; limited engagement, with some **uneven coverage** |
| **1–2** | Basic use of media language, **minimal** engagement; only basic understanding of intended audience, may lack relevance as a film opening or magazine | Production is basic, minimal understanding of codes; technical elements limited in success, production **may not be complete** | Basic research; limited planning meeting **few** requirements; implementation showing minimal understanding | Basic technical skills, **only one** creative approach, limited appeal to the audience | Minimal understanding; basic or obvious comment, minimal selection of examples; basic engagement, uneven coverage likely |
| **0** | No creditable content | No creditable content | No creditable content | No creditable content | No creditable content |

Three things are worth reading twice:

- **"Knowingly subverts" sits at the top with "accurately follows."** Breaking a convention on purpose and being able to say why scores as well as observing it perfectly.
- **The CCR is marked twice**: once for its own technical and creative skill (strand 4, AO3) and once for the quality of the evaluation in it (strand 5, AO2). A creative CCR that says nothing loses strand 5. A thoughtful CCR delivered as a read-aloud essay loses strand 4.
- **"All four questions"** is the phrase in strand 5's top three bands. Uneven coverage caps that strand at 3 or 4, regardless of how good the strongest answer is.

Marks are curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw.

## After the sit

- **Returned Tue 2026-12-01.** You band your own portfolio against these criteria before any mark is discussed. The conversation is about the gap between your band and the mark, not about the mark.
- You then write **one production target**: specific, evidenced from the feedback, achievable in Semester 2. "Hold focus in low light" beats "get better at filming". It is logged as LB4 and collected on in S2.
- The next assessment, [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-a4-section-a-authentic-format|A4]], sits Wed 2026-12-16.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **A2**, the blog mid-point | The same blog, already marked once. Its feedback is your instruction sheet |
| **CS7**, CCR draft review against the real criteria | Where the CCR stands, and your place in Wednesday's triage queue |
| The **Mon 11-02 screening and Tue 11-03 audit** | Real audience testimony on your product, and the pickup list from it |
| Wednesday's **submission checklist** | Run it yourself before Wednesday, so surgery time goes on the CCR rather than on admin |
| The four CCR questions | Coverage of all four is what strand 5's top bands require |

# 9607 S1 A4: Section A in Authentic Format

[[classes/media-studies/media-studies|Media Studies]] · [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-13-a4-section-a-in-authentic-format|Lesson 13]] · Attainment 4 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Wed 2026-12-16, the Wednesday double |
| Category | Attainment, the last of four in the 50% category. The Forecast Grade anchor |
| Format | Component 2 Section A in the real examination format |
| Timing | **30 minutes viewing and note-making, then 45 minutes writing** |
| Marks | 25, on the official Paper 2 five-criteria rubric |
| Assesses | AO1 and AO2 |
| Extract | Unseen TV-drama extract. Not a text taught to this class |
| Feeds | The End of Term Exam, and your Forecast Grade |
| Unit | [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-5-media-contexts\|U5 Media Contexts]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Use a **30-minute viewing window** to produce structured notes rather than a transcript.
2. Sustain a 45-minute write **from your notes**, not from memory of the extract.
3. Analyze how camera, sound, mise-en-scène and editing construct meaning in a text you have never seen.
4. Tie every observation to an effect, with examples precise enough that a marker can find them.
5. Bring context or critical debate to bear on the extract rather than bolting it on.

## The task

The same Section A question as A1, in the **authentic examination format**. That difference is the point of this assessment.

A1 was one hour of continuous writing. A4 splits the time the way the real paper does: **half an hour with the extract and your notes, then three quarters of an hour writing.** These are different skills. The viewing window rewards a note system; the writing window rewards working from that system instead of trying to re-watch the extract in your head.

The prompt is the Paper 2 Section A stem: analyze how the extract constructs meaning through camera, sound, mise-en-scène and editing.

## Instructions

1. **Conditions briefed once.** The format difference from A1 is stated explicitly, because it is what is being tested.
2. **30 minutes: viewing and notes.** The extract is screened on the examination's protocol. Build structured notes: a note grid or four-column chart by code family, not a running commentary. A transcript is a wasted half hour.
3. **45 minutes: writing.** From your notes. Do not expect another screening.
4. Hand in your script.

**How to spend the viewing window.** One pass to watch. Then passes that isolate one code family at a time. Count cuts where editing matters. Note the exact moment for anything you intend to quote, because strand 5 of the rubric is *use of examples* and a marker has to be able to find what you cite.

**If you are absent.** Contact your teacher **at least 24 hours before** the sitting. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

The **official Cambridge Paper 2 rubric**, the same five criteria used for A1 and the End of Term Exam. 25 marks, five criteria of 5, each banded **independently** on best fit.

| # | Criterion | AO | Marks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Media Concepts (language and representation) | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 2 | Contexts and Critical Debates (social significances) | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 3 | Use of Terminology | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 4 | Analysis of how meaning is created, including use of theory | AO2 | 0 to 5 |
| 5 | Use of Examples | AO2 | 0 to 5 |

Totals: **AO1 15, AO2 10.** Band words per criterion: **5** sophisticated or insightful · **4** thorough or effective · **3** clear or appropriate · **2** limited · **1** basic · **0** no creditable content.

### What each band looks like in this task

The criteria and band words are Cambridge's; the descriptions below are written for this course. They are the same descriptors used for A1, with one addition: at A4 the note-taking window is part of what is being assessed, so the top bands expect the coverage a note grid makes possible.

| Criterion | Band 5 | Band 3 | Band 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Media Concepts** | Reads language and representation together: technical choices are shown doing something to who or what is represented | Applies media language accurately, but representation is handled separately or briefly | Concepts are named without being applied to this extract |
| **Contexts and Critical Debates** | Genre, industry or audience context explains a specific choice, and any theory is tested against the extract including where it strains | One relevant context is stated and connected to at least one choice | Context is asserted and left unconnected |
| **Use of Terminology** | Precise throughout, sound and editing included | Correct on camera and mise-en-scène, thinner on sound and editing | Everyday description with occasional labels |
| **Analysis of meaning** | Every observation reaches an effect. Nothing is listed | Most observations reach an effect, some stop at description | What happens is described, meaning left implied |
| **Use of Examples** | Specific timed moments from **all four** code families, findable from your description alone | Real examples, unevenly distributed across code families | Examples general, or about the extract as a whole |

Marks are curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw. A4 is the **Forecast Grade anchor**: it is the single piece of evidence weighted most heavily when your forecast is set, because it is the most authentic sitting of the semester.

## After the sit

- Scripts back within **five working days**, with **AO splits recorded** so you can see which AO is your gap rather than only your total.
- Self-assessment against the mark scheme before any discussion of marks, as at A1.
- One logged target, retrieved at the End of Term Exam.
- The [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-eot-component-2-paper|End of Term Exam]] sits in the window Mon 2027-01-11 to Mon 01-18. A4 is its rehearsal in miniature: Section A of the same paper. These dates may shift when the school publishes the calendar for that period.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **A1** and its feedback | The same question, different clock. Your A1 target is checked here |
| **CS8**, guided Section A with the mark scheme open (Wed 12-09) | The direct rehearsal, one week before, with the rubric visible |
| Your note grid or four-column chart | The viewing window's whole purpose. Practise it before the day |
| The **strain log** and your theory cards | Criterion 2, contexts and critical debates |
| Mon and Tue of Lesson 13, one institution end to end | Industry context you can actually use on an extract |

# 9607 S1 End of Term: Component 2 Paper

[[classes/media-studies/media-studies|Media Studies]] · [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-16-end-of-term-exam-and-return|Lesson 16]] · End of Term Exam category, 20%

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | In the school exam window, **Mon 2027-01-11 to Mon 2027-01-18**. Your slot is set by the exam office |
| Category | End of Term Exam, 20% of the semester grade |
| Format | The **full Component 2 paper**, 2 hours, in the exam venue |
| Structure | Section A: unseen extract analysis (25) · Section B: contexts essay (25) |
| Marks | 50 |

These dates may shift when the school publishes the exam calendar for this period.

## Objectives

This exam asks you to show that you can:

1. Sit a full two-hour paper applying the minute budget you rehearsed, rather than working it out under pressure.
2. Analyze an unseen extract to the Section A standard you reached at A4.
3. Write a Section B contexts essay: a sustained argument using your own case study, built from research rather than recall.
4. Read your own AO breakdown afterwards and state your gap without prompting.

## The task

The full Component 2 paper, in the format and duration of the real examination. This is the only genuine two-hour sitting of the semester, which is why it happens in the school exam window rather than in a lesson.

**Section A**, 25 marks. An unseen moving-image extract, analyzed for how it constructs meaning through camera, sound, mise-en-scène and editing. The same task as A1 and A4, with the same rubric.

**Section B**, 25 marks. A contexts essay. This part is new: it draws on your own case study, which must be **student-built and less than five years old**, and on the audience, industry and regulation material from Unit 5.

## Instructions

1. **Your slot and venue come from the exam office.** Check them.
2. **Bring nothing.** No notes, no case-study document. Section B runs on what you built and learned.
3. **Apply the minute budget from the Lesson 15 rehearsal.** Two hours across two 25-mark sections means neither section can be allowed to eat the other.
4. **Section A**: use the screening protocol as at A4. Notes first, then write.
5. **Section B**: plan before writing. HW2's essay plan was practice for exactly this.

**If you are absent.** An exam-window absence goes through the exam office as well as your teacher, and the 24-hour advance-contact rule still applies (AL Student Guide p.8). This is a 20% category: a missed sitting is not a small problem.

## Rubric

### Section A, 25 marks

The **official Paper 2 five-criteria rubric**, identical to A1 and A4:

| # | Criterion | AO | Marks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Media Concepts (language and representation) | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 2 | Contexts and Critical Debates (social significances) | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 3 | Use of Terminology | AO1 | 0 to 5 |
| 4 | Analysis of how meaning is created, including use of theory | AO2 | 0 to 5 |
| 5 | Use of Examples | AO2 | 0 to 5 |

### Section B, 25 marks

The **same five criteria**, applied to the contexts essay. Section B is marked on the identical grid, so the habits that earn marks in extract analysis earn them in the essay too. Terminology, examples and analysis-tied-to-effect are assessed either way. What changes is where the evidence comes from: your case study rather than an extract on screen.

### The bands

Per criterion, on both sections: **5** sophisticated or insightful · **4** thorough or effective · **3** clear or appropriate · **2** limited · **1** basic · **0** no creditable content. Best fit, and each criterion is banded independently.

Across the paper: **AO1 60%, AO2 40%.**

Marks are curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw. This is the 20% End of Term category, summative on previously covered content.

## After the exam

- **Tue 2027-01-19: scripts returned** with **question-level AO breakdowns**, not just a total.
- **Wed 2027-01-20, the double:** you convert that data into a **one-page Semester 2 target sheet**: where the marks went, which AO is your gap, and one action. It is logged as LB7, and it needs to be specific enough to act on months later.

| **A1 and A4** and their AO splits | Two Section A attempts already marked on this rubric, with your gap named |
| Your own case study | Student-built, under five years old, and the backbone of Section B |

# PAL S1 A1: Final Observational Drawing

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-05-a1-the-final-observational-drawing|Lesson 05]] · Attainment 1 of 5

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Wed 2026-09-30, one double (about 90 minutes) |
| Category | Attainment, the first of five in the 50% category |
| Format | Made in class. You finish the drawing you started in W4, at the same station |
| Submitted | The drawing **and** the written reflection, together, at the close |
| Marked on | Observation · Tone · Composition · Reflection |
| Feeds | The mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29 |
| Returned | Within five working days |
| Unit | [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-1-drawing-and-the-visual-elements\|U1 Drawing and the Visual Elements]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Draw what you can actually see, including the parts that are difficult.
2. Use the **full range of tone**, from your lightest light to your darkest dark.
3. Use texture only where the surface asks for it, not everywhere.
4. Resolve your edges and your cast shadows.
5. Write a reflection that says **what you did**, not how you felt about the result.

## The task

You finish the observational drawing you have been building since W4. Same station, same objects, same drawing. One double to take it from decided-everywhere to finished.

Then you write one page of reflection in your sketchbook.

Both are submitted together at the close. **A1 is a drawing and the evidence that you can see what you did.** The reflection is part of the assessment, not an afterthought.

## Instructions

**Working order** (a checklist, not a script):

1. Push the **full tonal range first**. Get your darkest darks in before caution sets in.
2. Texture passes, where the surface demands them.
3. Edges and cast shadows.
4. Step back at arm's length **twice**: at about 20 minutes and about 50 minutes.

**The rules for the day.** From the start of the double it is your eyes and your paper. No phones. No looking at your neighbour's drawing. Your teacher will circulate and ask questions ("where is your darkest dark?") but will not put hands on your drawing today.

**The reflection.** One page, full sentences, at least four of these five:

- "I chose this viewpoint because …"
- "The light comes from …, so the darkest tones are …"
- "The texture I am most happy with is … because …"
- "The hardest part was …"
- "Next time I will …"

**Unfinished at the end is submitted at the end.** The double is the time there is.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before** the class. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without telling anyone in advance the mark may be 0, even if you were genuinely ill (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

Four criteria, equally weighted. Each is judged on its own, so a strong tonal range does not cover a weak composition.

| | **Observation** | **Tone** | **Composition** | **Reflection** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | Drawn from looking throughout, including the difficult parts. Proportions and relationships are convincing without being measured | Full range in use, from lightest light to darkest dark, with the mid-tones carrying the form. Texture appears only where the surface asks for it | The viewpoint is a decision you can explain. The drawing sits on the page deliberately, and the negative space works | Names specific decisions and their reasons. Identifies a real weakness precisely |
| **Confident** | Mostly drawn from looking. A few passages fall back on what you expected to see | Wide range, darkest darks present, edges resolved. Texture mostly earns its place | The viewpoint works and the placement is considered | Names decisions clearly, with reasons. The weakness named is real but general |
| **Competent** | Drawn from looking, with the easy parts stronger than the difficult ones | Mid-range throughout. The darkest darks are not fully dark, so the form flattens a little | The composition is sound but not chosen: the object sits where it happened to land | Says what was done. Reasons are thin |
| **Adequate** | Some observation, some copying of what you assumed the object looks like | A narrow band of tone. Little separation between light and shadow | The drawing floats, or crowds one edge | Describes feelings about the result more than decisions in the work |
| **Limited** | Little evidence of looking at the actual object | Tone is applied flatly or hardly at all | No compositional decision is visible | One or two sentences, unconnected to the work |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a **curved grade**, not a raw score. G10 curves are more generous than G11: the grade reflects where you are on the way somewhere, not what this drawing would score at A Level.

## After the sit

- Back within **five working days**, with written feedback.
- A1 feeds the **mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29**.
- **Keep the drawing.** With your day-one garlic drawing it is the before-and-after pair for the mid-term conversation and for parents' evening.
- **HW1 is set today:** at least 20 photographs of **one** subject over the National Day break, varied viewpoint and varied light, no editing, due Wed 2026-10-14. It opens Unit 2. No class next Wednesday.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS1**, the exercise set (contour, tonal, texture, negative space) | The four skills A1 asks for, each already practised and marked |
| **L04**, composing the final drawing | The viewpoint and placement decisions. They are assessed |
| Weeks 1 to 4 of your sketchbook | The tonal scales and texture studies. Bring the book |
| The reflection frames above | Write better sentences by knowing the frames in advance |

# PAL S1 A2: Photographic Series

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-09-a2-the-photographic-series|Lesson 09]] · Attainment 2 of 5

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Wed 2026-11-04, one double (about 90 minutes) |
| Category | Attainment, the second of five in the 50% category |
| Format | Made in class from photographs you already took. **No new shooting today** |
| Submitted | A series of **6 to 8 images**, titled, plus the written reflection, posted to MB by the close |
| Marked on | Framing · Viewpoint · Light · Series thinking |
| Also collected | Contact sheet and annotated rejects, into the sketchbook as process evidence |
| Returned | Within five working days |
| Unit | [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-2-photography\|U2 Photography]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Select 6 to 8 images from many, so that **removing any one costs the series something**.
2. Reject an off-theme frame **even when it is the prettiest one you have**.
3. Sequence images so the order carries meaning: an opener, a development, a closer.
4. Title the series so the title makes a claim rather than a label.
5. Write a reflection that accounts for the selection you made.

## The task

The shooting is done. Today is selection, sequence and words.

You arrive with all your frames, your contact sheet and your edits. You leave with a series of 6 to 8 images, in a deliberate order, with a title and a reflection, posted to MB.

The test of a series, and you will be asked it at the start:

- Take any one image away. **Does the group lose something?**
- Add your prettiest off-theme frame. **Does the group get worse?**

If you can answer both, you understand what you made.

## Instructions

**1. Selection (about 30 minutes).** Two forced passes:

- **The kill-your-darlings pass.** Your strongest image that does not serve the theme comes out. It goes into the sketchbook with a note explaining why, not into the series.
- **The weakest-link pass.** If an image needed two sentences of defending, replace it or cut it.

**2. Sequencing (about 20 minutes).** Order is meaning. Choose an **opener** that invites, a **development** that varies, a **closer** that lands. Lay out two different orders side by side, gallery view or prints on the table, and keep the one that reads better when you say it aloud.

Then title it. A title is a claim, not a label: *Nobody Uses the Front Door* does more work than *Doors of Building B*.

**3. Reflection (about 20 minutes).** One page, full sentences:

- "My series is about …"
- "I chose these … from … frames because …"
- "The strongest image is … because …"
- "My viewpoint or light decision that worked best was …"
- "If I shot the theme again I would …"

**4. Submit.** Series, title and reflection to MB. Contact sheet and annotated rejects into the sketchbook.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

Four criteria, equally weighted, each judged on its own.

| | **Framing** | **Viewpoint** | **Light** | **Series thinking** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | Every frame is composed on purpose. What is left out is as deliberate as what is in | Viewpoints vary because the subject needed them to, and you can say why each one was chosen | Light is used, not just present. The quality and direction of light does work in the images | Removing any image costs the series something. The order builds. The title makes a claim the pictures support |
| **Confident** | Consistently well framed, with one or two frames that drifted | Real variety of viewpoint, mostly motivated | Light is noticed and mostly controlled | A clear series with a logic you can explain. The order is considered |
| **Competent** | Competent framing. Some frames are centred by default rather than by choice | Some variety, but several frames share the same easy viewpoint | Light is adequate: correctly exposed, not yet used expressively | A group of related images. Order is sensible but not doing much work |
| **Adequate** | Framing is inconsistent. Distracting elements are left in the frame | Little variety. The subject is photographed the same way repeatedly | Light is whatever it was on the day | Images share a subject but not an idea. Any one could be swapped out without loss |
| **Limited** | Little evidence of framing decisions | One viewpoint throughout | Light is a problem the images have rather than a tool they use | A collection, not a series |

**Series thinking is the criterion that separates this from a photo album.** The same judgment reappears at A3, at the portfolio, and in every A Level unit after it.

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade, not a raw score, with the more generous G10 curve.

## After the sit

# PAL S1 A3: Final Collage

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-14-a3-the-final-collage|Lesson 14]] · Attainment 3 of 5

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Wed 2026-12-09, one double (about 90 minutes) |
| Category | Attainment, the third of five in the 50% category |
| Format | Made in class. You finish the collage built across W14 and W15 |
| Submitted | The collage **and** the written reflection, at the close |
| Marked on | Juxtaposition · Layering · Composition · Meaning |
| Also collected | Drafts, dry-fit photographs and scraps, into the sketchbook as process |
| Returned | Within five working days |
| Unit | [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-3-collage\|U3 Collage]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Put two images together so that the **pairing** says something neither says alone.
2. Layer deliberately, so depth and order carry meaning.
3. Finish the top layer, the edges and any words under assessment conditions.
4. **Remove anything that is only decoration**, and know it by testing it.
5. Write a reflection that points at decisions visible in the work.

## The task

You finish the collage. The last layer goes down and the work starts speaking for itself.

The test from Lesson 10, asked one final time before you submit:

**Cover any one element with your hand. Does the collage lose part of its sentence?**

If a piece is only decoration, it comes off.

A3 is a made-in-class attainment. **The mark rewards decisions you can point to**, in the work and in the reflection. Meaning is judged on both: the collage has to carry it, and the reflection has to give the reasons.

## Instructions

1. Finish the **top layer**, then the **edges**, then any **words**.
2. Run the covering test on every element. Anything that survives only because it looks nice comes off.
3. Write the reflection: one page, full sentences, pointing at things a reader can see in the work.
4. Submit collage and reflection together at the close.
5. Put your drafts, dry-fit photographs and leftover scraps into your sketchbook. They are process evidence for SB2 and A5.

**One main idea.** Your collage should be able to be summed up in one sentence. You wrote that sentence in Lesson 12. It is what makes "meaning" markable rather than a matter of taste.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

Four criteria, equally weighted, each judged on its own.

| | **Juxtaposition** | **Layering** | **Composition** | **Meaning** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | Pairings produce something neither image held alone. The joins are chosen, and surprising in a way you can justify | Layers create real depth and a reading order. What is buried and what is on top are decisions | The whole surface is composed. Scale shifts do work. Nothing is where it landed by accident | One idea, carried by the work itself. The reflection adds reasons rather than supplying the meaning |
| **Confident** | Pairings clearly do work together, with one or two that only sit next to each other | Layering is deliberate and mostly controlled | Composed, with a considered focal point and edges | The idea is clear in the work. Reflection explains it well |
| **Competent** | Some pairings say something; others are simply adjacent | Layers exist but mostly stack rather than interact | Sound composition, not yet using scale or the whole surface | An idea is present but you need the reflection to find it |
| **Adequate** | Images are placed together without a relationship between them | Little layering, or layering that hides rather than builds | Elements are distributed evenly with no emphasis | The reflection asserts a meaning the work does not carry |
| **Limited** | A group of cut-out images | Single layer, or accidental overlap | No compositional decision visible | No idea identifiable in work or writing |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade, not a raw score, with the more generous G10 curve.

# PAL S1 A4: Final Poster

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-16-a4-the-final-poster|Lesson 16]] · Attainment 4 of 5

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Wed 2026-12-23, one double (about 90 minutes). The last teaching session before the winter break |
| Category | Attainment, the fourth of five in the 50% category |
| Format | Made in class, from a thumbnail you already decided. **Handmade or digital**, your choice |
| Submitted | The poster **and** the written reflection, at the close |
| Marked on | Hierarchy · Typography · Message · Audience |
| Also collected | Thumbnails and type studies, into the sketchbook as process |
| Returned | Within five working days |
| Unit | [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-4-graphic-design-and-the-poster\|U4 Graphic Design and the Poster]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Execute a decided thumbnail as a finished poster, in whichever medium you chose.
2. Build a **hierarchy**: make the eye arrive in the order you intend.
3. Set type so it is legible and so the type choice suits the message.
4. Deliver **one message to one audience** within three seconds and three meters.
5. Write a reflection naming the hierarchy decisions you made.

## The task

One double, one poster, made from a thumbnail you decided last week. The design thinking has already happened, so these 90 minutes are execution with judgment.

The standard is the unit's own test:

**Pin it up. Walk back three meters. Count three seconds. If the message does not land in that window, no amount of craft saves it.** That is the whole assessment in one sentence.

## Instructions

1. Work from your **chosen thumbnail**. This is not the session to redesign.
2. Build the hierarchy first: what the eye hits first, second, third.
3. Set the type. Legibility at three meters beats decoration at arm's length.
4. Finish the surface, handmade or digital.
5. **Run the three-second test yourself** before you submit. Pin it up, walk back, look.
6. Write the reflection: one page, naming your hierarchy decisions and why you made them.
7. Submit poster and reflection together. Thumbnails and type studies into the sketchbook.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). This is the **last session before the winter break**, so a missed A4 is difficult to reschedule.

## Rubric

Four criteria, equally weighted, each judged on its own.

| | **Hierarchy** | **Typography** | **Message** | **Audience** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | The eye arrives exactly where you intended, in the order you intended. Scale, weight, position and space all working together | Type choice suits the message and is legible at three meters. Spacing and alignment are controlled | One message, unmistakable in three seconds, and worth saying | A specific audience is visible in every choice: the language, the image, the tone |
| **Confident** | Clear first, second and third read. One element competes slightly | Legible and well set, with a type choice that suits the message | One clear message, landing inside the window | A clear audience, addressed consistently |
| **Competent** | A focal point exists, but the second and third reads are muddled | Legible. The type choice is neutral rather than chosen | The message is understandable, though it takes longer than three seconds | An audience is implied but generic |
| **Adequate** | Elements compete. The eye does not know where to start | Legibility problems: too small, too tight, or fighting the background | The message needs explaining | No particular audience is addressed |
| **Limited** | No hierarchy: everything is the same weight | Type is hard to read at any distance | No identifiable message | No audience considered |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade, not a raw score, with the more generous G10 curve.

## If your class takes the printmaking route

Unit 4 runs **either** Graphic Design **or** Printmaking, in the same slot. The poster is the default; your teacher will confirm the route in class. If your class takes the [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-u4-printmaking-variant|printmaking variant]], then **A4 is the final linocut print** instead, on the same date, with the same notice and the same weight. Its criteria:

| | **Carving control** | **Ink and registration** | **Two-tone legibility** | **Reflection** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | Marks are cut with intent: line weight varies for a reason, and the cutting itself carries the image | Even ink, clean registration across the edition. The print quality is repeatable | The two tones separate the image cleanly and read at distance | Names specific decisions in the carving and printing, and what the proof taught you |
| **Confident** | Controlled cutting, with a few passages where the tool led rather than followed | Good ink coverage, registration accurate with minor drift | The image reads clearly in two tones | Clear reasons, evidenced from the proof |
| **Competent** | Competent cutting. Line weight is fairly uniform | Ink is adequate; registration is visible but off | The image reads, with some tonal confusion | Says what was done |
| **Adequate** | Cutting is uneven or tentative | Patchy ink, registration noticeably out | The two tones fight each other | Describes the process without decisions |
| **Limited** | Little control of the tool | The print is incomplete or illegible | No tonal separation | Minimal writing |

Everything else on this page applies either way. **CS4 changes with the route too**: proof plus annotation instead of thumbnails plus poster analysis.

## After the sit

- Back within **five working days**, with written feedback.
- The poster (or print) returns as **portfolio material at W19**, so keep it in good condition.
- **Over the break:** keep the sketchbook alive, 2 to 3 pages a week. **A5 collects it on Wed 2027-01-06.** Read the portfolio spec before that session.

| Where it came from | What to use it for |

| **CS4**, thumbnail set + poster analysis (Wed 2026-12-16) | The direct rehearsal, one week before, and where your chosen thumbnail comes from |

## Objectives

The sketchbook is the only assessment in this course that cannot be produced in a session. It asks one question: **is there evidence, across a whole semester, of somebody thinking in a book?**

Specifically it asks whether you can show:

1. Ideas that developed rather than arrived.
2. Experiments, including the ones that failed.
3. Visual research: things you looked at, recorded and used.
4. Reflection written as you went, not summarized at the end.
5. A book somebody else can navigate.

## The task

Hand in the sketchbook. That is the whole task.

What should be in it, accumulated since Week 1:

- Weekly work from every session, dated.

- Collage drafts, dry-fit photographs and scraps from U3.

- Whatever you did over the National Day and winter breaks, dated.

**You have already been shown this standard twice**, at the SB1 and SB2 spot-checks. A5 is the same book, judged completely rather than sampled.

## Instructions

1. Bring the book on Wed 2027-01-06.
2. Before you hand it in, **number your pages** if they are not numbered, and make sure everything is dated.
3. Do not tidy it by removing failures. A sketchbook with no failed experiments in it evidences less, not more.
4. Do not add three weeks of work the night before. Dated work made on the day is the point, and the difference is visible.
5. Hand it in at the close, with the portfolio.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). This is the last teaching session of the semester, so there is no later class to hand it to.

Five criteria, **weighted**:

| Criterion | Weight |

| Experimentation | 25% |
| Visual research | 20% |
| Critical reflection | 15% |
| Presentation | 15% |

| | **Ideas and creativity** (25%) | **Experimentation** (25%) | **Visual research** (20%) | **Reflection** (15%) | **Presentation** (15%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | Ideas visibly develop across pages: a thought is followed, tested, changed. Personal direction is emerging | Wide, genuine experimenting, including failures kept and annotated. The experiments feed the finals | Sustained looking, recorded and then used. Sources are noted and something is taken from each | Written as you went, naming decisions and what changed because of them | Navigable, dated, complete. The order tells the story of the semester |
| **Confident** | Ideas develop, with some jumps unexplained | Regular experimenting across media, mostly connected to the finals | Consistent visual research, mostly used | Regular reflection with clear reasons | Well kept, dated, easy to follow |
| **Competent** | Ideas are present but arrive rather than develop | Some experimenting, in the media the unit required | Visual research is collected and only sometimes used | Reflection after the big pieces, thinner in between | Complete, with some undated or unordered stretches |
| **Adequate** | Little development: mostly finished attempts side by side | Experimenting is thin, or confined to one medium | Copied or collected images with nothing taken from them | Occasional writing that describes rather than reflects | Gaps, undated pages, difficult to follow |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade, not a raw score, with the more generous G10 curve.

There is no preparing for A5 in the last week. It is prepared by keeping it every week, which is the reason the weekly MB posting exists.

# PAL S1 End of Term: Semester Portfolio

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-lesson-17-the-portfolio-and-the-sketchbook|Lesson 17]] · End of Term Exam category, 20%

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Due | Wed 2027-01-06, submitted at the close of the last teaching session |
| Category | End of Term Exam, 20% of the semester grade |
| Format | **One organized file**: PDF, PowerPoint or Keynote. There is no sitting and no exam |
| Contains | Your 4 to 5 strongest works, each with supporting material you choose |
| Reviewed | During the exam window, Mon 2027-01-11 to Mon 2027-01-18 |
| Marked on | Selection · Sequence · Supporting evidence · Presentation quality · The argument |
| Returned | Wed 2027-01-20, the return session |
| Submitted alongside | The [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/assessments/pal-s1-a5-sketchbook\|A5 sketchbook]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. **Select** your strongest work, which means judging your own work honestly.
2. Sequence a semester so it reads as development rather than as a pile.
3. Choose, for each final piece, the supporting material that best shows how you got there.
4. Produce one organized file that meets basic image-quality standards.
5. Say what your portfolio **argues** about your development, not only what is in it.

## The task

You have four finished pieces (drawing, photographic series, collage, poster or print), a semester of process work, and forty-plus sketchbook pages. The task is to turn that into **one organized portfolio that argues something you can see**.

What goes in:

- **Your 4 to 5 strongest works.**
- For each one, **supporting material you choose**: process photographs, drafts, contact sheets, thumbnails, experiments.
- Everything to the image-quality rules in the portfolio spec, in one file, in a deliberate order.

The double on Wed 2027-01-06 is for assembling and submitting it. The semester ends the way every unit in it ended: **by choosing.**

## Instructions

1. **Select** the 4 to 5 works. If you have exactly four finals, the fifth slot is yours to use for a piece of process work or an experiment you want seen.
2. For each, choose supporting material. One or two well-chosen items beat everything you have.
3. **Photograph or scan** anything physical properly. A badly lit photograph of a good collage is a badly lit collage as far as a portfolio is concerned.
4. Assemble one file, in order, following the spec's checklist.
5. Write the **one thing your portfolio argues**: a sentence about your development that the sequence supports.
6. Submit at the close, with your sketchbook.

**Order is an argument.** Chronological is the obvious choice and it is a legitimate one, because it shows development. But it is not the only one, and if you choose another order you should be able to say why.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). This is the semester's last teaching session, so there is no later class.

## Rubric

Five criteria, equally weighted.

| | **Selection** | **Sequence** | **Supporting evidence** | **Presentation quality** | **The argument** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | The genuinely strongest work, chosen with honest judgment, including one piece a weaker student would have hidden | The order makes development visible. Each piece sets up the next | Each final is supported by exactly the material that shows how it was reached. Nothing padding | Clean file, good images, consistent, easy to move through | States what the semester shows about you, and the portfolio proves it |
| **Confident** | Strong work, well judged, with one questionable inclusion | A clear, deliberate order | Good supporting material throughout, with some over-inclusion | Well presented, minor inconsistencies | A clear claim the portfolio mostly supports |
| **Competent** | Reasonable selection, defaulting to the four finals | Chronological, without much thought about it | Some support for some pieces | Complete and legible, with variable image quality | A general statement about improving |
| **Adequate** | Selection includes work that does not belong | Order appears accidental | Supporting material is thin or unrelated | Poor images, inconsistent layout, hard to navigate | No argument, just contents |
| **Limited** | Incomplete selection | No order | No supporting material | The file is difficult to open or read | Nothing stated |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade, not a raw score, with the more generous G10 curve.

## Why there is no exam

A studio course has nothing to sit: there is no paper and no content to recall under timed conditions. The 20% is met by **the portfolio you submit on the last teaching session, reviewed during the exam window.** You do not sit anything, and there is no PAL session during the window. It is a submission, not a sitting.

## After submission

- Reviewed during the window, Mon 2027-01-11 to Mon 2027-01-18.
- Returned **Wed 2027-01-20** with grades, comments and one-to-one feedback, alongside A5.
- Together with A5 this produces the semester's final grades.
- **Keep the file.** In G11 the same act of selection and sequencing becomes the Component 1 portfolio, marked by Cambridge.

## How to prepare

| Where to look | What to use it for |

| The portfolio spec | The 4 to 5 works rule, the image-quality rules, and the checklist. Read it over the break |
| All four attainment reflections | You have already written about each piece. Mine them for the argument |
| Your sketchbook | Where the supporting material lives. This is why the rejects and drafts were kept |
| A2's selection and sequencing work | The same skill at semester scale. You have done this once already, with six to eight photographs |
